1.pericope_label: No condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus: the law of the Spirit of life

schools.summary: Gill notes that the apostle, having discoursed largely in the preceding chapter concerning the struggle and combat believers feel within themselves, and having opened the true causes and reasons of the saints’ grievances and complaints and of what gives them the greatest uneasiness in this life, proceeds here to take notice of the solid ground and foundation they have of spiritual peace and joy, which arises from their justification and adoption, the purposes and decrees of God, and particularly the everlasting and unchangeable love of God in Christ, the source and spring and security of all. The following phrase he calls of difficult interpretation, and allows that the words may be understood of the Gospel revealing and declaring deliverance from the law of Moses, so that there can be no condemnation by it. The Gospel may be designed by the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus, and may be called a law not as succeeding the law of works, by which that is abrogated, nor as requiring conditions to be performed or enjoining duties to be observed or delivering out threatenings in case of disobedience, but as it is a doctrine and an order and chain of truths. Calvin explains the transition: after having described the contest which the godly have perpetually with their own flesh, the apostle returns to the consolation which was very needful for them and which he had before mentioned, namely that though they were still beset by sin they were yet exempt from the power of death and from every curse, provided they lived not in the flesh but in the Spirit. He joins together three things: the imperfection under which the faithful always labour, the mercy of God in pardoning and forgiving it, and the regeneration of the Spirit; and this last he sets in place so that no one should flatter himself with an empty notion of pardon while remaining unchanged. On the following verse he says it is a confirmation of the former sentence, and that its meaning depends on noticing the words: using a language not strictly correct, by the term law the apostle designates the Spirit of God, who sprinkles our souls with the blood of Christ, not only to cleanse us from the stain of sin with respect to its guilt but also to sanctify us that we may be really purified. He adds that the Spirit is called life-giving, the genitive case being taken after the manner of the Hebrew as an adjective; and it hence follows that they who detain a man in the letter of the law expose him to death, while the Spirit who quickens is set free from that letter.

Henry begins with what he calls one signal privilege of true Christians, and describes the character of those to whom it belongs. The verse is the apostle’s triumph after that melancholy complaint and conflict in the foregoing chapter, where sin was remaining, disturbing and vexing, but, blessed be God, not ruining; and he observes that the apostle takes the complaint to himself but humbly transfers the comfort, with himself, to all true believers, who are all interested in it. It is the unspeakable privilege and comfort of all those that are in Christ Jesus that there is therefore now no condemnation to them, Henry insists, and he presses the force of the word therefore, since the ground of the comfort lies in what has gone before: the very struggle described in the previous chapter, so far from proving a man condemned, is itself a mark of the life that has been given him. He takes the description that follows as marking out who these are, those who walk not after the flesh but after the Spirit, and holds that this is not a condition to be performed in order to obtain the privilege but the character by which those who have it may be known; the privilege is theirs by their being in Christ, and the walk is the evidence of it. He draws the practical consequence that the believer’s comfort is to be sought not in the absence of inward conflict, which will continue, but in the union with Christ which secures him against condemnation while the conflict lasts.

Clarke prefixes an analysis of the whole chapter, tracing the happy state of those who believe in Christ and walk under the influence of his Spirit, the design of God in sending his Son to redeem men from sin, the miserable state of the carnally minded, how Christ lives and works in his followers with their blessedness here and their happiness hereafter, the sufferings which are the common lot of all men and from which Gentiles and Jews alike have the hope of being finally delivered, the use and importance of hope, and the intercession of the Spirit. On the second verse he identifies the law of the Spirit of life as the Gospel of the grace of Christ, which is not only a law or rule of life but affords that sovereign energy by which guilt is removed from the conscience, the power of sin broken, and its polluting influence removed from the heart. He sets the contrast sharply: the law was a spirit of death, by which those who were under it were bound down, because of their sin, to condemnation and death, whereas the Gospel proclaims Jesus the Saviour, and what the law bound unto death it looses unto life eternal. Wesley says that there is now no condemnation either for things present or past, and marks the turn in the argument, that the apostle now comes to deliverance and liberty, resuming the thread of his discourse which had been interrupted earlier in the previous chapter. On the second verse he is brief to the point of bluntness: the law of the Spirit is the gospel, and the law of sin and death from which it has freed him is the Mosaic dispensation.

Barnes prefaces the chapter with a general estimate, that it is one of the most interesting and precious portions of the sacred Scriptures, that some parts of it are attended with great difficulties but its main scope and design are apparent to all. It is a continuation of the subject discussed in the previous chapter and is intended mainly to show that the gospel could effect what the law was incapable of doing, since in that chapter the apostle had shown that the law was incapable of producing sanctification or peace of mind, having traced its influence on the mind in different conditions. On the second verse he explains that the word law means that rule, command or influence which the Spirit of life produces, since a law often means anything by which we are ruled or governed; and he sees no reason to doubt that Spirit here refers to the Holy Spirit, the phrase the Spirit of life meaning the Holy Spirit producing or giving life, that is giving peace and joy and activity and salvation, in opposition to the law spoken of in the previous chapter which produced death and condemnation. Ellicott notes that the Apostle had already, at the end of the last chapter, touched the confines of that state of deliverance and of liberty which he is now going on to describe, so that the opening of this chapter is connected in form with the close of the last; the intervention of Christ puts an end to the struggle waged within the soul. The condemnation which in the present and final judgment of God impends over the sinner, he says, is removed by the intervention of Christ and by the union of the believer with him, and by that union the power and empire of sin are thrown off. The second verse he calls a statement of the great antithesis of which the rest of the section is a development, between the law of the Spirit of life and the law of sin and of death; the first phrase defines more fully the mode in which the union with Christ becomes operative in the believer, since it begins by imparting to him the Spirit of Christ, this Spirit creates within him a law, and the result of that law is life, that perfect spiritual vitality which includes within itself the pledge of immortality. The Spirit he takes as the Spirit of Christ, which is hardly as yet conceived of as a distinct person in the argument. Robertson notes the two particles of the opening and says they point back to the triumphant note at the close of the previous chapter after the preceding despair. As sinners, he says, we deserved condemnation in our unregenerate state in spite of the struggle, but God offers pardon to those in Christ Jesus, and this is Paul’s Gospel; the fire has burned on and around the Cross of Christ, and there and there alone is safety, so that those in Christ Jesus can lead the consecrated, the crucified, the baptised life. On the second verse he defines the phrase as the principle or authority exercised by the Holy Spirit which bestows life and which rests in Christ Jesus, parses the verb of liberation as a first aorist active indicative of an old verb, and notes that two of the chief manuscripts read thee instead of me, adding that it matters little, since we are pardoned, we are free from the old law of sin and death, and we are able by the help of the Holy Spirit to live the new life in Christ. Lightfoot’s note attached here in fact anticipates a word from later in the chapter, the term rendered vanity, which he says is not unfitly so translated but is improperly applied to the vanishing, changeable, dying state of the creation; for the word does not so much denote the vanishing condition of the outward state as the inward vanity and emptiness of the mind, as when the apostle says of the Gentiles that they became vain in their imaginations, and that the Gentiles walk in the vanity of their mind.

Theodoret takes the opening verse as a statement about the changed condition of the will. There is now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh but after the Spirit, he says, for our passions can no longer get the mastery over us without our own consent, now that we have received the grace of the Spirit of God. The point he presses is not that the passions have been abolished but that their compulsion has been broken, so that what was formerly a tyranny is now at most a solicitation which requires the consent of the man himself before it can prevail; and it is on that ground, rather than on any claim of sinlessness, that the sentence of condemnation is said to be lifted. On the second verse he sets the two laws in exact parallel: as the apostle had just before called sin the law of sin, so now does he call the life-giving Spirit the law of the spirit of life. The grace of Christ, received by faith, he says has bestowed on the believer a double freedom, for it has not only overthrown the power of sin but put an end also to the tyranny of death; and he takes the verses that follow as the apostle’s demonstration of how that second overthrow was accomplished, so that the two clauses of this verse govern the argument of the whole passage.

debates: What the law of the Spirit of life means: Gill calls the words of difficult interpretation and allows that the Gospel may be so designated, defending the name of law against three misunderstandings, Clarke likewise identifies it with the Gospel of the grace of Christ and Wesley states this flatly, while Barnes and Robertson refer the term to the Holy Spirit himself and the rule he exerts, Ellicott traces a sequence from union with Christ through the imparted Spirit to an inward law and so to life, and Calvin grants that the language is not strictly correct since the Spirit of God is what is called a law

What the law of sin and death is: Wesley identifies it with the Mosaic dispensation, Clarke with the law as a spirit of death binding men to condemnation, and Theodoret with sin itself, which the apostle had just so named, so that the freedom conferred is double, from the power of sin and from the tyranny of death

On what ground condemnation is removed: Ellicott makes it the intervention of Christ and the believer’s union with him, Robertson the pardon offered at the Cross to those in Christ, Theodoret the fact that the passions can no longer prevail without consent, and Henry the standing privilege of all who are in Christ, of which the walk after the Spirit is the mark rather than the condition
outliers: Barnes calls the chapter one of the most interesting and precious portions of Scripture, some parts attended with great difficulties
Robertson says the fire has burned on and around the Cross, and there alone is safety
Robertson notes the variant reading thee for me and judges that it matters little
Lightfoot’s note here argues about the word rendered vanity in a later verse, that it denotes emptiness of mind rather than a vanishing outward state

3.pericope_label: What the law could not do: God sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh condemned sin in the flesh

schools.summary: Gill works carefully through what is not meant before settling what is. It is not to be understood of the law of the mind in opposition to the law of sin, which indeed is very feeble and impotent, since man had a power originally of obeying the divine commands but through sin has lost his strength, and even a renewed mind cannot perform what it would, which is owing to the flesh or corrupt nature; that mind has strong desires after holiness and after keeping all the commandments of God, but these desires cannot be fulfilled by it, and without Christ it can do no good thing. Nor is the ceremonial law intended, though that too is weak. The moral law is meant, which is weak not in itself but through the flesh. On the following verse he takes the righteousness of the law to mean not the righteousness of the ceremonial law, though that was fulfilled by Christ, but of the moral law, which requires holiness of nature and righteousness of life and death in case of disobedience; active righteousness, that is obedience to the precepts of the law, is what is designed. This is what the law requires, obedience to its commands being properly righteousness, and by Christ’s obedience to it we are made righteous, which gives the title to eternal life; and this is said to be fulfilled in us, not by us. Calvin calls the passage the polishing or adorning of the proof that the Lord has by his gratuitous mercy justified us in Christ, the very thing which it was impossible for the law to do, and says that since this is a very remarkable sentence every part of it must be examined. That the apostle treats here of free justification, or of the pardon by which God reconciles us to himself, he infers from the last clause; for if Paul intended to teach that we are prepared by the spirit of regeneration to overcome sin, why was that addition made? On the clause about the righteousness of the law being fulfilled he is emphatic: they who understand that the renewed, by the Spirit of Christ, fulfil the law introduce a gloss wholly alien to the meaning of Paul, for the faithful, while they sojourn in this world, never make such a proficiency that the justification of the law becomes in them full or complete. This then must be applied to forgiveness; for when the obedience of Christ is accepted for us, the law is satisfied, so that we are counted just, since the perfection which the law demands was exhibited in our flesh, and for this reason, that its rigour should no longer have the power to condemn us. But as Christ communicates his righteousness to none but those whom he joins to himself by the bond of his Spirit, Calvin holds that the walking after the Spirit which follows is not the ground of the justification but the mark of those to whom it belongs.

Clarke enumerates what the law could not do: it could not pardon, it could not sanctify, and it could not dispense with its own requisitions, being the rule of righteousness and therefore bound to condemn unrighteousness, which is its unalterable nature. Had there been perfect obedience to its dictates, he says, instead of condemning it would have applauded and rewarded; but as the flesh, the carnal and rebellious principle, had prevailed and transgression had taken place, the law was rendered weak and inefficient to undo this work of the flesh and to bring the sinner into a state of pardon and acceptance with God. On the following verse he takes the fulfilment in both its parts: that the guilt might be pardoned through the merit of that sacrifice, and that we might be enabled, by the power of his own grace and Spirit, to walk in newness of life, loving God with all our heart and soul and mind and strength and our neighbour as ourselves; and thus the righteousness, the spirit, the design and the purpose of the law is fulfilled in us, through the strength of the Spirit of Christ, which is here put in opposition to the weakness of the law through the flesh. He notes further that the concluding clause of the verse is textually the same as one that occurs earlier, and weighs the question of its authenticity there. Wesley identifies the law as that of Moses and its weakness as an incapacity for conquering our evil nature, and argues that if it could have done so God need not have sent his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh. We with our sinful flesh, he says, were devoted to death; but God, sending his own Son in the likeness of that flesh though pure from sin, condemned that sin which was in our flesh, gave sentence that sin should be destroyed and that the believer should be wholly delivered from it. On the following verse he takes the righteousness of the law as the holiness it required, fulfilled in those who are guided in all their thoughts and words and actions not by corrupt nature but by the Spirit of God; and he observes that from this place onward St Paul describes primarily the state of believers, and that of unbelievers only to illustrate this.

Barnes identifies the law here as the law of God, the moral law, and says it could not free from sin and condemnation, as the apostle had fully shown in the previous chapter. It was weak, that is feeble and inefficacious, and could not accomplish this, in consequence of the strength of sin and of the evil and corrupt desires of the unrenewed heart; but the fault was not in the law, which was good, but was owing to the strength of the natural passions and the sinfulness of the unrenewed heart. On the following verse he takes the righteousness of the law to mean that we might be conformed to the law or be obedient to its requirements, and no longer under the influence of the flesh and its corrupt desires, so that the fulfilment spoken of is our being obedient or complying with its demands. Ellicott states the whole argument of the verse compactly: precisely on that very point where the law of Moses showed its impotence, namely in the attempt to get rid of sin, which it failed to do because of the counteracting influence of the flesh, precisely on this very point God interposed, by sending his Son in a body of flesh similar to that in which sin resides, and as an offering to expiate human sin, and so dethroned and got rid of sin in the flesh which he had assumed; the flesh, the scene of its former triumphs, became now the scene of its defeat and expulsion. The opening phrase he renders literally as the impossible thing of the Law. On the following verse he says the consequence of this was a great change: hitherto the Law could not be kept because of the antagonistic influence of the flesh, henceforth it may be kept for the reason that this influence has ceased and that its place is taken by the influence of the Spirit. The righteousness he defines as the just requirement of the Law, its due and rightful claims, and the fulfilment in us as meaning that we might be examples of its fulfilment; those who walk not after the flesh he explains as those who direct their conduct not as the flesh would guide them but according to the dictates and guidance of the Spirit, that is the indwelling Spirit of Christ. Robertson renders the opening literally as the impossibility of the law, as shown in the previous chapter, and notes that it stands either as a nominative absolute or an accusative of general reference with no syntactical connection with the rest of the sentence; the verb of weakness he parses as an imperfect, the law having continued weak as already shown. On the likeness of sinful flesh he refers to the parallel in Philippians and explains that it was a real man, but more than man, since he was God’s own Son; the two genitives mean flesh of sin, that is flesh marked by sin, which the flesh of man is but the flesh of Jesus is not. On the following verse he renders the noun as the requirement of the law, parses the purpose clause with the first aorist passive subjunctive, and says Christ met it all in our stead; the two ways of walking he calls the two laws of life, the one described in the previous chapter and the other in this, and he takes the Spirit to be most likely the Holy Spirit or else the renewed spirit of man.

Theodoret defends the law while conceding its impotence. The law then was not evil, but good, though impotent, he says, and that weakness arose from its injunctions being given to those encumbered with a mortal nature; for now, by the thrice-holy baptism, we have received the pledge of immortality, which is precisely what those under the law lacked. On the likeness he is the most exact of the commentators: the apostle says not in the likeness of flesh, but in the likeness of sinful flesh, for he received actually the human nature, but human sin he received not; wherefore that which he thus assumed he calls not the likeness of flesh but the likeness of sinful flesh, the word likeness qualifying the sinfulness and not the flesh. On the following verse he takes the fulfilment as accomplished by Christ on our behalf: he has paid our debt, says Theodoret, and fulfilled that which the law aimed at. And what then was this? To render them righteous that had received that law. From this he draws a conclusion in the law’s favour: if the dispensation of Christ Jesus has brought to effect the intention of the law, then the law deserves not blame but praise, since its purpose has been achieved by another means and not abandoned.

debates: What the fulfilment of the righteousness of the law in us means: Calvin denies outright that it can describe anything the believer performs, calling that reading a gloss wholly alien to the meaning of Paul, since the faithful never reach such proficiency in this life, and refers the clause to forgiveness, the obedience of Christ being accepted for us; Gill likewise grounds it on Christ’s obedience imputed, and Theodoret says Christ paid our debt and fulfilled what the law aimed at, while Ellicott reads it of an actual keeping now possible because the antagonistic influence of the flesh has ceased, Clarke takes it of pardon and of a renewed walk together, and Barnes and Wesley of obedience and holiness in the believer

What the likeness of sinful flesh qualifies: Theodoret insists the apostle deliberately did not write the likeness of flesh, since the human nature was really assumed while human sin was not, so that likeness attaches to the sinfulness alone; Robertson reaches the same result grammatically, that the genitives describe flesh marked by sin, true of man’s flesh but not of Christ’s

Which law is meant by what the law could not do: Gill excludes both the law of the mind and the ceremonial law in favour of the moral law, Barnes agrees, Wesley identifies it as the law of Moses, and all of them locate the weakness in the flesh rather than in the law itself, Theodoret adding that the injunctions were laid on men encumbered with a mortal nature
outliers: Ellicott turns the flesh from the scene of sin’s triumphs into the scene of its defeat and expulsion
Robertson notes that the opening phrase has no syntactical connection with the rest of the sentence at all
Theodoret argues that the law deserves praise rather than blame, since its aim has been achieved by another means
Clarke observes that the closing clause of the second verse repeats one found earlier, and weighs its authenticity

5.pericope_label: They that are after the flesh mind the things of the flesh: the carnal mind is enmity against God

schools.summary: Gill defines what is meant by flesh as the corruption of nature, and is careful about who is said to be after it: not all that have flesh in them, for the best of saints have it in them and regenerating grace does not remove it, there being a difference between being in the flesh, being after the flesh, and flesh being in us; those meant are such as are still as they were born, who have nothing but flesh or corrupt nature in them. On the carnal mind he says the phrase includes the best part of corrupt man, the mind, the understanding, the judgment, the will, the affections, the thoughts and the reasonings of man, and may be rendered the wisdom or prudence of the flesh, so called to distinguish it from that wisdom which is from above and from the natural and civil wisdom which is laudable. On the enmity he takes the words as giving the reason why the issue of carnal mindedness is death, namely that the carnal mind is not only an enemy but enmity itself against God: against his being, since it reasons against it, wishes he was not, forms unworthy notions of him, thinks him such a one as itself, and endeavours to bury him in forgetfulness and erase him out of the mind. On the conclusion he notes only that those said here to be in the flesh are the same who were earlier said to be after it and are there described. Calvin explains why the antithesis is introduced: not only to confirm, by an argument derived from what is of an opposite character, what he had before mentioned, that the grace of Christ belongs to none but those who, having been regenerated by the Spirit, strive after purity, but also to relieve the faithful with a seasonable consolation, lest, being conscious of many infirmities, they should despair. On the word rendered carnally minded he reviews the renderings: Erasmus has given affection and the old translator prudence, but since it is certain that the apostle’s term is the same as what Moses calls the imagination or devising of the heart, and that under this word are included all the faculties of the soul, reason, understanding and affections, it seems to Calvin that minding, that is thinking or imagining or caring, is the more suitable word. He observes further that the apostle begins with two characters, the carnal and the spiritual, taking the first because it is first as to us in order of time, and that here he does not reverse the order as he sometimes does, but goes on first with the carnal man and then describes the spiritual. On the conclusion he says it is not without reason that he has rendered the adversative particle as an illative, for the Apostle infers from what had been said that those who give themselves up to be guided by the lusts of the flesh are all of them abominable before God; and he has thus far confirmed this truth, that all who walk not after the Spirit are alienated from Christ, for they are without any spiritual life.

Clarke makes the distinction of the verse a historical one, calling it the great distinction between Jews and genuine Christians: the former are after the flesh, under the power of the carnal, rebellious principle, and consequently relish the things of the flesh, the things which appertain merely to the present life, having no relish for spiritual and eternal things, while they that are after the Spirit are under the influence of the Spirit of God. To be carnally minded he explains as living under the influence of the carnal mind, which is to live in a state of condemnation and consequently to be liable to death eternal, whereas on the contrary he who is spiritually minded has the life and peace of God in his soul and is in full prospect of life eternal. On the enmity he says the carnal mind is so called because it relishes earthly and sinful things and lives in opposition to the pure and holy law of God, and that this enmity is irreconcilable and implacable hatred. He explains the impossibility that follows with an argument from the nature of the thing: the carnal mind will come under no obedience, for it is sin and the very principle of rebellion, and therefore it cannot be subject nor can it be made so while it remains what it is. On the conclusion he says that because this carnal mind is enmity against God, they that are in the flesh, who are under the power of its workings, as every soul is that has not received redemption in the blood of the Lamb, cannot please God, because of the rebellious workings of this principle of rebellion and hatred; and if they cannot please God they must be displeasing to him, and consequently in the broad road to destruction. Wesley describes those after the flesh as remaining under the guidance of corrupt nature, having their thoughts and affections fixed on such things as gratify it, namely on things visible and temporal, on things of the earth, on pleasure of sense or imagination, on praise or riches, while those after the Spirit are under his guidance and think of the things of the Spirit. To be carnally minded, he says, is the sure mark of spiritual death and the way to death everlasting, while to be spiritually minded is a sure mark of spiritual life and the way to life everlasting, attended with peace, the peace of God which is the foretaste of life everlasting and peace with God set against the enmity that follows. That enmity he directs against God’s existence, power and providence.

Barnes takes those after the flesh as under the influence of the corrupt and sinful desires of the flesh, that is the unrenewed, who are supremely devoted to the gratification of their corrupt desires, while those after the Spirit are under its influence and led by it. On the carnal mind he explains that following the inclinations of the flesh or the corrupt propensities of our nature leads to condemnation and death, and calls the expression one of great energy, since it shows that this not only leads to death, or leads to misery, but that it is death itself, there being woe and condemnation in the very act and purpose of being supremely devoted to the gratification of the flesh. The enmity he takes as the reason for the previous verse, which had affirmed that to be carnally minded was death without stating why; it is now explained by saying that it is enmity against God and thus involves a sinner in conflict with him and exposes him to his condemnation. On the conclusion he says the words follow as a consequence: those in the flesh are unrenewed sinners who follow fleshly appetites and desires and are not led by the Spirit of God, and while they are thus in the flesh, while they thus pursue the desires of their corrupt nature, they cannot please God. Ellicott sharpens the description of those after the flesh: they are men who not only walk, that is direct their conduct, according to the promptings of the flesh, but who are in themselves and in the whole bent of their dispositions the slaves of these promptings, so that their whole mental and moral activity is set upon nothing else but the gratification of these cravings of sense; the phrase rendered who mind, he notes, is not confined to the exercise of the intellect. The following verse he would translate as for the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace, and explains that to think of nothing but the gratification of the senses is in itself death, that dead condition of the soul which issues in eternal death, while on the other hand to have the thoughts and affections governed solely by the Spirit brings with it that healthful, vital harmony of all the functions of the soul which is a sure pledge of life. The enmity he compresses into a syllogism, that the carnal mind is death because it implies enmity with God and enmity with God is death; and the conclusion he prefers to render with a simple conjunction rather than an inference, saying that neither can it be expected that those who are absorbed in the things of sense should be able to please God. Robertson glosses the verb rendered do mind as a present active indicative meaning to think or to put the mind upon a thing, and refers to the contrast between flesh and Spirit drawn out in the letter to the Galatians. The noun in the following verse he renders as the bent or will of the flesh, which is death as shown in the previous chapter, set against life and against the peace described earlier in the epistle. On the enmity he parses the verb of subjection as a present passive of a late verb, a military term for subjection to orders, and says the present tense here means continued insubordination, while the clause that follows means that it is not even able to do otherwise; this helpless state of the unregenerate man, he observes, the apostle has shown above apart from Christ, and hope lies in Christ and the Spirit of life. On the conclusion he gives the reason as the handicap of the lower self in bondage to sin, but enters a caution: this does not mean that the sinner has no responsibility and cannot be saved, for he is responsible and can be saved by the change of heart through the Holy Spirit.

Theodoret reads the antithesis as a statement about what a man follows and therefore becomes. Taking the Spirit here to mean the grace of the Spirit, he sets beside the verse the parallel from the letter to the Galatians, that if we live in the Spirit let us also walk in the Spirit, and teaches that he who follows that grace both thinks and does the things agreeable to it, while he that is enslaved to the flesh does the contrary; the minding described is therefore not a bare opinion but the whole direction of a life. On the following verse he is careful about the terms: the apostle says not the flesh, but the inclination of the flesh, that is the breaking forth of the passions, for the recompense of sinners is death; and the inclination of the Spirit is life and peace, for he who lives after the Spirit gains peace with God. On the enmity he says the apostle again condemns the inclination of the flesh, that is the tyranny of the passions, which he declares are at variance with God; and he turns the impossibility that follows into a question that answers itself, how it is possible that he who has admitted the tyranny of the passions should embrace the service of God, while yet choosing to serve sin. The force of the argument for Theodoret lies in that word tyranny: what is condemned is not the body or its natural appetites but a usurped rule under which a man has placed himself, and it is the incompatibility of two services, not any defect in the creature, that makes the subjection impossible.

debates: Who are meant by those after the flesh: Gill distinguishes carefully between being in the flesh, being after it, and having flesh in us, since the best of saints have it and grace does not remove it, so that the description fits only those who remain as they were born; Ellicott presses the same point from the other side, that these are men whose whole disposition is enslaved to the promptings of sense, while Clarke turns the contrast into one between Jews and genuine Christians

How the word rendered carnally minded should be translated: Calvin reports affection from Erasmus and prudence from the old translator, and prefers minding on the ground that the term answers to what Moses calls the imagination of the heart and covers reason, understanding and affections together; Gill reaches the same breadth by enumeration and allows the rendering wisdom of the flesh, Robertson calls it the bent or will of the flesh, and Theodoret the inclination, that is the breaking forth of the passions

Whether the carnal mind merely deserves death or is death: Barnes insists the expression means that it is death itself and not only its cause, calling the phrase one of great energy, and Ellicott agrees that to live for the gratification of the senses is in itself that dead condition of soul which issues in eternal death, while Clarke and Wesley speak rather of a state of condemnation and a sure mark of spiritual death
outliers: Robertson notes that the verb for subjection is a military term for obedience to orders, and that the present tense marks continued insubordination
Robertson cautions that the impossibility does not remove the sinner’s responsibility or his hope of being saved
Calvin says the antithesis was introduced partly to console the faithful, lest their consciousness of many infirmities drive them to despair
Theodoret turns the incapacity into a question about serving two masters rather than a defect in the creature

9.pericope_label: Ye are in the Spirit, if the Spirit of God dwell in you: the body dead because of sin, the Spirit life

schools.summary: Gill takes the opening as a change of address, meaning that these are not carnal but spiritual men, not in a state of unregeneracy but in a state of grace, and treats the indwelling of the Spirit as the reason proving it. On the indwelling of Christ he is careful to distinguish it from other modes of presence: it is not as Christ is in the whole world and in all his creatures, nor circumscriptively and to the exclusion of himself elsewhere, for his person is above in heaven, his blood is within the veil, his righteousness is upon his people, and his Spirit and grace are in them; so he comes to be in them, being formed in their hearts by the Spirit of God in regeneration, when the Father reveals him not only to them but in them. On the quickening of the mortal body he rejects the reading of some, that it means the continued work of sanctification in the heart by the Spirit; for regeneration and not sanctification is signified by quickening, and that quickening occurs when the Spirit first takes up his dwelling in the soul. Besides, he adds, the apostle had already spoken of the life of the spirit or soul, and it is mortal bodies and not the soul that are here in question, so that the resurrection of the body is what is promised. Calvin observes that the apostle applies hypothetically a general truth to those to whom he was writing, not only that by directing his discourse to them particularly he might more powerfully affect them, but also that they might with certainty gather from the description already given that they were of the number of those from whom Christ had taken away the curse of the law; and at the same time, by explaining what the Spirit of God works in the elect and what fruit he brings forth, he sets a mark by which the genuine may be known. On the indwelling of Christ he says that what he had before said of the Spirit he now says of Christ, in order that the mode of Christ’s dwelling in us might be intimated; for as by the Spirit he consecrates us as temples to himself, so by the same he dwells in us. He then explains more fully what he had referred to before, that the children of God are counted spiritual not on the ground of a full and complete perfection but only on account of the newness of life that is begun in them. On the last verse he calls it a confirmation of the preceding, derived from the efficient cause: since by the power of God’s Spirit Christ was raised, and since the Spirit possesses eternal power, he will also exert the same with regard to us; and he takes it as granted that in the person of Christ was exhibited a specimen of the power which belongs to the whole body of the Church, making God the author of the resurrection and assigning to him what properly belongs to him.

Henry says that in these verses the apostle represents two more excellent benefits which belong to true believers, of which the first is life. The happiness described is not barely negative, not merely a not being condemned, but positive, an advancement to a life that will be the unspeakable happiness of the man. He states the equivalence of the two indwellings in a line: if the Spirit be in us, Christ is in us, for he dwells in the heart by faith. He then takes the verses as telling us what becomes of the bodies and the souls of believers, and holds the two halves of the tenth verse to be a division of the man rather than a contradiction: the body must die, and dies because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness, so that what sin has forfeited in the one, righteousness has secured in the other. The eleventh verse he treats as extending the benefit to the body after all, since the same Spirit who is now the pledge of life in the soul will hereafter quicken the mortal body also, and the resurrection of Christ is both the ground and the pattern of it. He draws from the whole the practical comfort that the believer need not fear what death can do to the body, since the Spirit who dwells in him is the earnest of its recovery.

Clarke identifies those addressed as Christians who have believed in Christ Jesus as the sin offering which has condemned sin in the flesh, and who, having been justified by faith and made partakers of the Holy Spirit, are enabled to walk in newness of life. He prefers to render the conditional particle as seeing that rather than if so be that, and notes the reversal of their former condition: the flesh, the sinful principle, dwelt in them before, and its motions were the proofs of its indwelling, but now the Spirit dwells in them and his motions are the proofs of his. On the indwelling of Christ he calls it the criterion by which the state of grace may be judged: if Christ dwell in the heart by faith, the body is dead in reference to sin, the members of the body no more performing the work of sin than the body of a dead man performs the functions of natural life; or else, he allows, the apostle may mean that although because of sin the life of man is forfeited and the sentence that dust thou art stands, yet the spirit is life because of righteousness. On the last verse he says it confirms the sense given to the preceding: he who here receives the grace and Spirit of Christ, and continues to live under its influence a life of obedience to the divine will, shall have a resurrection to eternal life, and the resurrection of Christ shall be the pattern after which they shall be raised; and he notes the variant reading in the closing phrase. Wesley glosses being in the Spirit as being under his government, and the not having the Spirit of Christ as his not dwelling and governing in a man; such a one, he says, is none of his, not a member of Christ, not a Christian, not in a state of salvation, and he calls this a plain, express declaration which admits of no exception, adding that he who hath ears to hear, let him hear. On the indwelling of Christ he states the equivalence briefly, that where the Spirit of Christ is, there is Christ. The body he says is devoted to death because of sin heretofore committed, while the spirit is already truly alive because of righteousness now attained; and he observes that from the thirteenth verse onward St Paul, having finished what he had begun earlier in the epistle, describes purely the state of believers.

Barnes takes the opening as the opposite character to that just described, showing the power of the gospel: these are not under the full influence of corrupt desires and passions but are spiritually minded, under the direction and influence of the Holy Spirit, who is often represented as dwelling in the hearts of Christians. On the indwelling of Christ he calls the expression evidently figurative, the word Christ being used to denote his spirit and his principles, that is, his influence over the man; literally he cannot be in a Christian, but the close connexion between him and Christians, and the fact that they are entirely under his influence, is expressed by this strong figurative language, which is not infrequently used elsewhere. On the last verse he grounds the argument on two things: first on the power of God, since he that had power to restore Christ to life has power to give life to them, and secondly on the connexion between Christ and his people, since he that did in fact restore him to life will also restore them, as when our Lord said that because he lives they shall live also. Ellicott observes that the two terms, the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ, are used as convertible, and that the Spirit of Christ is indeed the presence of Christ himself in the soul, comparing the promise that the Father would give another Comforter to abide with them for ever and the assurance that he would not leave them comfortless. On the tenth verse he takes the word for the body’s death of physical death and marks its limit sharply: the doom entailed by sin still indeed attaches to the body, but only to the body, for the body must die, but there the hold of sin upon the Christian ends and it cannot touch him further; turning then to the highest part and faculty of human nature, the spirit, he finds it alive because of righteousness. On the last verse he says this vitality extends beyond the grave and will even react upon that material body which had just been spoken of as given over to death: die it must, but the same Spirit to which the soul owes its life will also reinfuse life into the dead body, just as the body of Christ was itself raised from the dead. On the closing phrase he judges the balance of authority to be in favour of the reading because of his Spirit, calling the other an Alexandrian correction. Robertson says the readers are not sold under sin any more, takes the second phrase as probably meaning in the Holy Spirit, and insists that what is taught here is not Pantheism or Buddhism but the mystical union of the believer with Christ in the Holy Spirit; the conditional particle he renders if as is the fact, and he observes that the Spirit of Christ is the same as the Spirit of God just before, finding in the interchange an incidental argument for the deity of Christ. On the tenth verse he says the body has the seeds of death in it and will die because of sin, and that the redeemed human spirit is called life rather than living, being God-begotten and God-sustained life. On the last verse he parses the future active of a late verb meaning to make alive, notes the variant reading because of the Spirit found in several manuscripts, and judges that both ideas are true though the genitive is slightly more probably correct.

Cyril of Jerusalem uses the interchange of titles in this passage to establish that the Spirit is one and the same though called by different names. That the Holy Spirit and the Comforter are the same, he says, is declared in the words which identify the Comforter as the Holy Ghost; and that the Comforter is the same as the Spirit of Truth is declared when the Lord promises another Comforter to abide for ever, even the Spirit of Truth. The multiplication of titles, he insists, is no multiplication of persons, and the readers are to hold the unity firmly against any conclusion drawn from the variety of names. On the quickening of the mortal body he gathers testimonies to the resurrection of Christ as the ground of ours, recalling the warning not to ask who shall ascend into heaven or descend into the deep to bring up Christ from the dead, the charge to remember Jesus Christ raised from the dead, and the argument that if Christ be not risen the preaching is vain and the faith vain, and that the apostles would then be found false witnesses of God because they testified that he raised up Christ. Theodoret guards the earlier verse against a misreading: it is evident that they who received these instructions were not devoid of the body itself, but what the apostle means is that they were conquerors over the fleshly passions and enjoyed the grace of the thrice-holy Spirit resident within them, just as our Lord says in a similar sense that his disciples are not of the world, not that they came from elsewhere. On the tenth verse he says the apostle makes clear what had been ambiguous and shows that it was not the mere flesh itself that he is condemning but sin, for he bids the body be dead with regard to sin, that is, not to commit sin, and by the spirit he here means the soul in its having become already spiritual, enjoining that righteousness be followed after. On the last verse he says the apostle invigorates them by hope of the future and inspires them with a willing readiness sufficient for present contests, since before long their bodies will be immortal and superior to the passions that now molest them, and this will be done by the same God of all who now sustains them.

debates: How the closing phrase of the eleventh verse should be read: Ellicott judges the balance of authority to favour because of his Spirit and calls the alternative an Alexandrian correction, while Robertson reports the same two readings, allows that both ideas are true, and thinks the genitive slightly more probably correct; Clarke also notes the variant

What the death of the body means: Ellicott takes it of physical death and marks its limit, that the doom of sin still attaches to the body but only to the body and there sin’s hold on the Christian ends, Robertson says it carries the seeds of death, Theodoret takes it of being dead to sin, that is not committing it, and Clarke allows both readings, either that the members no longer perform sin’s work as a corpse performs no natural function, or that the life of man is forfeited

In what sense Christ may be said to be in the believer: Barnes calls the expression figurative and denies that Christ can literally be in a Christian, Gill distinguishes the indwelling from Christ’s presence in the world and locates his person in heaven and his blood within the veil while his Spirit and grace are within, Calvin makes the Spirit the mode of the indwelling, and Henry simply equates the two, that where the Spirit is, Christ is
outliers: Robertson finds in the interchange of the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ an incidental argument for the deity of Christ, and denies that the union taught is Pantheism or Buddhism
Cyril of Jerusalem gathers the titles of the Spirit to prove that Comforter, Holy Ghost and Spirit of Truth name one and the same
Wesley calls the declaration that a man without the Spirit is none of Christ’s a plain statement admitting no exception
Theodoret notes that the readers were not bodiless but had become conquerors over the passions, as the disciples are not of the world without coming from elsewhere

12.pericope_label: We are debtors, not to the flesh: as many as are led by the Spirit of God are the sons of God

schools.summary: Gill notes that the appellation brethren is not used because they were so by nation or by blood, though many in the church at Rome were Jews, nor merely in a free and familiar way of speaking, but rather on account of church membership and especially because they were in the same spiritual relation to God and Christ; and its use shows the apostle’s great humility and condescension and his love and affection for them. On the warning he says that those who live after the flesh are dead while they live and shall die a second or eternal death if grace prevent not; and he raises the question whether one who has received the grace of God in truth can live after the flesh, answering that flesh or corrupt nature, though still in such a person, has not the dominion over him, and that to live in sin or in a continued course of sinning is contrary to the grace of God, though flesh may prevail and greatly distress. On the leading of the Spirit he says it is not by the spirit of the world, nor of the devil, nor by men’s own spirits, and explains the act of leading by two figures: it is either in allusion to the leading of blind persons, or of such as are in the dark, or rather to the leading of children and teaching them to go, which supposes life in those that are led and some degree of strength, though a good deal of weakness, and is a display of powerful and efficacious grace. Calvin calls the first verse the conclusion of what has been previously said, since if we are to renounce the flesh we ought not to consent to it, and if the Spirit ought to reign in us it is inconsistent not to attend to his bidding. He observes that the sentence is defective, the other part of the contrast being omitted, that we are debtors to the Spirit, but that the meaning is in no way obscure, and cites Pareus that the apostle did not mention it because it was so evident. On the following verse he says a threatening is added in order more effectually to shake off their torpor, by which also they are fully confuted who boast of justification by faith without the Spirit of Christ, though they are more than sufficiently convicted by their own conscience, for there is no confidence in God where there is no love of righteousness. It is indeed true, he grants, that we are justified in Christ through the mercy of God alone, but it is equally true and certain that all who are justified are also sanctified. On the leading of the Spirit he calls it a confirmation of what has immediately preceded, teaching that those only are deemed the sons of God who are ruled by his Spirit, for by this mark God acknowledges them as his own people; thus the empty boasting of hypocrites who without any reason assume the title is taken away, and the faithful are encouraged with unhesitating confidence to expect salvation, the import of the whole being that all those are the sons of God who are governed by his Spirit.

Clarke reports Dr Taylor’s view of the structure, that the apostle, having spoken separately both to Jews and Gentiles concerning holiness and the obligations to it, now addresses himself to both conjointly, drawing the general conclusion from all his arguments on the subject, then proving the validity of their claims to eternal life, and then meeting the difficulty that the affair of suffering persecution was a great stumbling block to the Jews. On the warning he allows that the Greek may mean that they shall afterwards die, and that this seems to indicate a temporal death, yet not exclusively of an eternal death, for both, and especially the latter, are necessarily implied. The mortifying he describes as seeking that grace and spiritual help which the Gospel of Christ furnishes, and resisting, and by resisting mortifying, the deeds of the flesh, against which the law gave no power. On the leading of the Spirit he is emphatic that no man who has not divine assistance can either find the way to heaven or walk in it when found; as Christ by his sacrificial offering has opened the kingdom of God to all believers, and as a mediator transacts the concerns of their kingdom before the throne, so the Spirit of God is the great agent here below to enlighten, quicken, strengthen and guide the true disciples of Christ. Wesley takes the deeds of the flesh to include not only evil actions but evil desires, tempers and thoughts, and the mortifying of them as killing and destroying these, with the promise of the life of faith more abundantly here and hereafter the life of glory. On the leading of the Spirit he adds that it is in all the ways of righteousness, and marks the turn in the argument: here St Paul enters upon the description of those blessings which he comprises later in the word glorified, though indeed he does not describe mere glory but that which is still mingled with the cross, the sum being through sufferings to glory.

Barnes says we owe the obligation as a matter of solemn duty, and sets out three grounds for it: that the Spirit dwells in us, that the design of his indwelling is to purify us, and that we are thus recovered from the death of sin to the life of religion, so that he who has imparted life has a right to require that it be spent in his service. We are not bound to indulge the corrupt propensities and passions, he adds, because they lead only to death. On the following verse he says that if a man lives to indulge his carnal propensities he will sink to eternal death, whereas what is required in the other clause can be accomplished only by the aid of the Holy Ghost, by cherishing and cultivating his influences; sin is mortified, he explains, when its power is destroyed and it ceases to be active, and the deeds of the body are the corrupt inclinations and passions. On the leading of the Spirit he says this introduces a new topic, illustrating the benefits of the gospel, namely that it produces a spirit of adoption; those led are such as submit to the Spirit’s influence and control, the Spirit being represented as influencing, suggesting and controlling, so that one evidence of piety is a willingness to yield to that influence and submit to him, while one decided evidence of the want of piety is an unwillingness to do so. Ellicott renders the first clause as meaning that we are under an obligation, and observes that in the lively sequence of thought the second clause of the antithesis is suppressed, the sense being that we are under an obligation not to the flesh but to the Spirit. On the following verse he renders the mortifying as meaning that under the influence of the Spirit you reduce to a condition of deadness and atrophy all those practices to which the impulses of your material nature would prompt you. Robertson notes that the word for debtors occurs elsewhere in Paul, and that the negative goes with the preceding verb rather than with the infinitive that follows. On the warning he parses the present indicative of the verb meaning to be about to do, rendering it that they are on the point of dying, and takes the death as eternal and the life promised as eternal life, the Spirit being named in the instrumental case. On the sons of God he says the phrase is used in the full sense of the term, notes that a different word for children appears two verses later, and concludes that no great distinction can be drawn between them, since the word is used in various ways in the New Testament: in the highest sense, true of no one else, Jesus Christ is God’s Son, while in the widest sense all men are the offspring of God, as the apostle showed at Athens.

Chrysostom fixes on the form of the exhortation rather than its substance. After showing how great the reward of a spiritual life is, and that it makes Christ dwell in us, and that it quickens our mortal bodies and wings them to heaven and renders the way of virtue easier, the apostle next fitly introduces an exhortation to this purpose, that we ought not to live after the flesh. But this is not what he says, Chrysostom observes, for he words it in a much more striking and powerful way, saying that we are debtors; and the change of expression turns a bare prohibition into the acknowledgment of a debt already incurred, so that the readers are not merely forbidden something but reminded what they owe. Theodoret puts the same thought in a sentence: having received salvation of Christ Jesus and been made partakers of the grace of the Spirit, to him we owe the debt of service. On the warning he explains living after the flesh as following the passions of the flesh, and takes the death threatened as that which is eternal; and from the promise attached to mortifying the deeds of the body he draws a comparison of the two covenants, that this is the superiority which grace has over the law, that the law points out what is right while grace has the Spirit in addition, as a helpmate. The distinction matters to him because the demand made of the believer is not lighter than the law’s but heavier, and the difference lies wholly in the assistance given, so that what was impossible under the one becomes possible under the other. Cyril of Jerusalem, gathering the prophetic titles of the Spirit, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and might, of knowledge and godliness and the fear of God, insists that these signify that the Spirit is one and undivided while his operations are various, and adds further testimonies that God has put his Spirit upon his servant and poured his Spirit upon the seed.

debates: What the suppressed half of the antithesis is: Ellicott and Calvin agree that the apostle leaves unsaid that we are debtors to the Spirit, Calvin citing Pareus that it was omitted because it was so evident, while Chrysostom finds the whole force of the verse in the substitution of a debt for a bare prohibition, and Barnes supplies three grounds on which the debt rests

Whether the death threatened is temporal or eternal: Clarke allows that the Greek may point to a temporal death but insists eternal death is necessarily implied and is the chief meaning, while Robertson and Theodoret take it simply of eternal death, and Gill says such men are dead while they live

Whether the word for sons here differs from the word for children below: Robertson concludes that no great distinction can be drawn, since the term is used in various ways, Christ being God’s Son in a sense true of no one else while in the widest sense all men are his offspring
outliers: Calvin turns the threatening against those who boast of justification by faith without the Spirit of Christ, since there is no confidence in God where there is no love of righteousness
Gill explains the leading of the Spirit by the leading of children learning to walk, which supposes life and some strength together with much weakness
Theodoret makes the superiority of grace over law consist not in a lighter demand but in the helpmate given
Cyril of Jerusalem gathers the prophetic titles of the Spirit to show that he is one and undivided while his operations are various

15.pericope_label: The Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry Abba, Father: heirs of God and joint-heirs with Christ

schools.summary: Gill denies that the spirit of bondage can be the Spirit of God, since this is just the reverse of his character, who is a free Spirit or a Spirit of liberty, and contrary to his work and office, which is to show a soul its state of bondage by nature and to deliver it out of it; and though fear may arise from the convictions of sin, this he removes by discoveries of love. On the inheritance he notes that children, whether natural or adopted, are heirs to their parents, and that according to the Roman laws, which some think the apostle here respects, this held whether they were male or female, whereas according to the Jewish laws females did not inherit except for want of male issue; and though Job’s daughters inherited with his sons, this was a peculiar case, which the Jewish writers say was on account of their worth and beauty. Calvin says the apostle now confirms the certainty of that confidence in which he had already bidden the faithful rest secure, and does this by mentioning the special effect produced by the Spirit: he has not been given for the purpose of harassing us with trembling or of tormenting us with anxiety, but on the contrary for this end, that having calmed every perturbation and restored our minds to a tranquil state he may stir us up to call on God with confidence. On the joint witness he observes that the apostle does not simply say that God’s Spirit is a witness to our spirit but adopts a compound verb, which might be rendered contest were it not that the Latin word has a different meaning; what Paul means is that the Spirit of God gives us such a testimony that, when he is our guide and teacher, our spirit is made assured of the adoption of God, since our mind of its own self, without the preceding testimony of the Spirit, could not convey to us this assurance. On the inheritance he argues from what is annexed, that our salvation consists in having God as our Father, since it is for children that inheritance is appointed, and God having adopted us as his children has at the same time ordained an inheritance for us; and he intimates what sort of inheritance it is, that it is heavenly and therefore incorruptible and eternal, such as Christ possesses, his possession of it taking away all doubt as to ours.

Henry describes this as a fourth illustrious branch of the happiness of believers, namely a title to the future glory, and says it is fitly annexed to our sonship, for as the adoption of sons entitles us to that glory, so the disposition of sons fits and prepares us for it. He marks the difference from human practice: in earthly inheritances the rule does not hold that if children then heirs, since only the firstborn are heirs, but the church is a church of firstborn, for they are all heirs. The inheritance he takes as an inheritance of God himself and with Christ, so that the saints’ portion is not merely a place or a condition but a person, and their title to it rests on the same adoption which has already been proved by the witness of the Spirit. He then turns to the condition annexed and refuses to soften it: the way to the crown lies through the cross, and those who would reign with Christ must be content first to suffer with him. Henry treats this not as a hard bargain but as part of the privilege, since to suffer with Christ is itself a mark of the relation and an evidence of the sonship, and the sufferings are made light by the certainty and the greatness of what follows.

Clarke sets the bondage historically: all that were under the law were under bondage to its rites and ceremonies, and as through the prevalence of corrupt nature, which the law gave no assistance to remove, they were often transgressing, they had forfeited their lives and were continually through fear of death subject to bondage, whereas believers in Christ Jesus were brought into another state. On the joint witness he identifies the Spirit as that same Spirit, the Spirit of adoption, that is the Spirit who witnesses this adoption, which can be no other than the Holy Ghost himself, and insists that it certainly cannot mean any disposition or affection of mind which the adopted person may feel; for such a disposition must arise from a knowledge of this adoption, and the knowledge of this adoption cannot be given by any human or earthly means. On the inheritance he says that the legitimate children alone can inherit the estate, and that this is not an estate to which they succeed in consequence of the death of a former possessor but is like the promised land, given by God himself and divided among the children of the family. The object of the inheritance he presses hardest: it is neither an earthly portion nor a heavenly portion, but God himself who is to be their portion, for it is not heaven they are to inherit but God, who is infinitely greater than heaven. Wesley identifies those addressed as real Christians and qualifies the bondage carefully, that the Holy Ghost was not properly a spirit of bondage even in the time of the Old Testament, yet there was something of bondage remaining even in those who then had received the Spirit; the word again he refers to the state of the Jews before. On the cry he notes that the word denotes a vehement speaking, with desire, confidence and constancy, and that the second title explains the first. On the joint witness he says the same Spirit bears witness with the spirit of every true believer by a testimony distinct from that of his own spirit or the testimony of a good conscience, and adds that happy are they who enjoy this clear and constant. On the inheritance he says the joint heirship lets us know that it is a great inheritance which God will give us, since he has given a great one to his Son; and the suffering with him he takes as suffering willingly and cheerfully, for righteousness’ sake, calling this a new proposition which refers to what follows.

Barnes explains the spirit of bondage as the spirit that binds, or the spirit of a slave, which produces only fear, since the slave is under constant fear and alarm, whereas the spirit of religion is that of freedom and of confidence, the spirit of children and not of slaves; the word again implies that in their former state under the law they were in a state of servitude. On the joint witness he gives three reasons for taking the Spirit here as the Holy Spirit: that this is the natural meaning of the expression, that it is of the Holy Spirit that the apostle is mainly treating, and that it would be an unnatural and forced construction to say of the temper of adoption that it bore witness; the witnessing itself he explains as testifying or giving evidence to our minds. On the inheritance he says that if we sustain the relation of sons to God we shall be treated as such and admitted to share his favours, an adopted son coming in for a part of the inheritance, and the expression heirs of God meaning that we shall be partakers of that inheritance which God confers on his people. Ellicott says the Greek for spirit of bondage corresponds very nearly to what we should naturally understand by the English phrase, such a spirit as would be found in slaves, and observes that the word spirit varies much in meaning in these verses, here denoting the dominant habit or frame of mind while in the next verse it is used both for the Spirit of God and the spirit of man; the phrase again to fear he explains as meaning so as to take you back under the old terrorism of the Law. On the joint witness he asks what the nature of this concurrent testimony is and answers that the self-consciousness of the believer assures him of his sonship, since the relation in which he feels that he stands to God he knows to be that of a son, but that besides this he is aware of an external objective cause for this feeling, and that cause is the influence of the Holy Spirit. On the inheritance he says one characteristic of the son is that he is his father’s heir, and so it is with the Christian, who has an inheritance of glory which he will share with Christ; but he must not be surprised if, before sharing the glory, he also shares the sufferings, since all who suffer for the sake of the gospel are regarded as suffering with Christ and drink of the cup that he drank of. Robertson refers the term for adoption to its fuller discussion in the letter to the Galatians and observes that both Jews and Gentiles receive this adoption into the family of God with all its privileges, the double use of Father being the child’s privilege. On the joint witness he notes that the grammatical gender of the word for Spirit is neuter, as here, but that the Greek used also the natural gender as we do exclusively, and warns that it is a grave mistake to use the neuter it or itself when referring to the Holy Spirit; the verb he parses as taking the associative instrumental case. On the inheritance he calls the compound for joint-heirs a late and rare double formation found in Philo, in an Ephesian inscription of the imperial period and in papyri of the Byzantine period, and observes that the apostle is fond of compounds formed with the preposition meaning together, three of them standing in this single verse.

Theodoret reads the verse as another comparison of the two covenants. Again he compares grace and the law, calling the institutions of the latter bondage while at the same time showing that the law was written by the grace of the Spirit; and he draws the necessary distinction, that it is not the thrice-holy Spirit itself that is here called the spirit of bondage, but the imposition of the law as effected by that holy Spirit. On the joint witness he distributes the two terms carefully: by the Spirit the apostle means the Holy Ghost himself, and by our spirit the grace, or spirit of adoption, given to us, for both are here expressed by the same common word; and what he means is that we put forth this prayer, thus claiming sonship in it, as led by the teaching of the Spirit, so that in doing it we cannot be blameworthy, since we do it according to the divine direction. On the inheritance he traces the ascending series: it was not enough that we should have been freed from bondage and enjoyed the grace of liberty, but moreover we have been blessed with the privilege of the adoption; nay, and not only are we called sons but heirs also of God, and joint heirs with Christ. He then explains why the two titles are joined: since not every son becomes the heir of his father, the holy apostle has done well to join the heirship expressly with the sonship, so that no one may suppose the second follows the first as a matter of course. Cyril of Jerusalem cites the verse among the many titles of the Holy Ghost, who is called the Spirit of holiness, the Spirit of adoption, and the Spirit of revelation, the variety of names again indicating variety of operation rather than of person.

debates: What the spirit of bondage is: Gill denies outright that it can be the Spirit of God, whose character is liberty and whose office is to deliver from bondage, Theodoret distinguishes the Spirit himself from the imposition of the law as effected by him, Ellicott takes the word of a dominant habit or frame of mind such as slaves would have, Barnes of the temper of a slave under constant alarm, and Wesley grants that even under the Old Testament the Holy Ghost was not properly a spirit of bondage though something of bondage remained

Whether the inward witness can be a disposition of the believer’s own mind: Clarke argues that it cannot, since any such disposition must arise from a knowledge of the adoption which no human means can supply, Barnes calls it forced to say of the temper of adoption that it bore witness, Calvin holds that the mind of itself could never convey the assurance, while Ellicott describes a concurrence of the believer’s self-consciousness with an objective cause outside it

What the inheritance consists in: Clarke insists it is neither an earthly nor a heavenly portion but God himself, since it is not heaven they inherit but God, Calvin describes it as heavenly, incorruptible and eternal, such as Christ possesses, Barnes as a share in what God confers on his people, and Theodoret notes that the apostle joined heirship to sonship because not every son becomes his father’s heir
outliers: Robertson warns that it is a grave mistake to render the Spirit as it or itself, though the Greek noun is neuter
Gill compares Roman and Jewish inheritance law on daughters, and calls the case of Job’s daughters peculiar
Henry observes that in earthly inheritances only the firstborn are heirs, while the church is a church of firstborn and all are heirs
Robertson finds the word for joint-heirs in Philo, in an Ephesian inscription and in Byzantine papyri, and notes three compounds with together in one verse

18.pericope_label: The sufferings of this present time not worthy to be compared: the earnest expectation of the creature

schools.summary: Gill takes the present time to mean the then present age in which the apostle lived, which was an age in which the people of God suffered much, as was foretold by Christ, and which was necessary for the confirmation of the Gospel; grace and strength answerable to their trials were given them, and the power of God was visibly to be seen in supporting them. On the creature he reports the view of some who understand the universe, all created beings animate and inanimate, which having suffered much by the sin of man are introduced by a rhetorical figure as waiting for deliverance and a restoration to their paradisiacal estate; but he objects that some part of the world is manifestly distinguished from them in the verses that follow. He reports also the opinion of others that angels are here meant, who being obliged to minister to the heirs of salvation are said to wait for their manifestation. Calvin pauses first on the connecting particle, denying that it can be causal here since nothing has been previously said for which a reason is given, and holding that in such a case it has only an affirmative sense, or is to be viewed as a particle of transition or of addition, this latter meaning being perhaps the suitable one. On the creature he says the apostle teaches us that there is an example of the patience to which he had exhorted us even in mute creatures; and, omitting the various interpretations, he understands the passage to mean that there is no element and no part of the world which, being touched as it were with a sense of its present misery, does not intensely hope for a resurrection. He observes that two things are laid down, that all creatures are in distress, and that they are nevertheless sustained by hope; and he draws the argument for the readers, that if the insensible parts of the world can wait patiently under a burden they did not bring on themselves, much more should those wait who know both the cause of the present misery and the certainty of the deliverance.

Henry sets the two estimates against each other. The sufferings of the saints, he says, strike no deeper than the things of time, last no longer than the present time, are light afflictions and but for a moment; and he remarks how vastly different are the sentence of the word and the sentiment of the world concerning the sufferings of this present time. The glory to be revealed he treats as so far outweighing them that no comparison is possible, and he presses that the apostle does not say the sufferings are not real or not sharp but that they are not worthy to be compared, which is an argument about proportion rather than about feeling. On the following verse he observes that indeed the whole creation seems to wait with earnest expectation for the period when the children of God shall be manifested in the glory prepared for them, and he takes this universal expectancy as an argument to the believer: if the inanimate world is represented as leaning forward toward that day, those who are themselves the objects of the expectation should not be found indifferent to it. He draws the practical use that present suffering is to be measured not by what it costs now but by what it prepares, and that the certainty of the glory is what makes patience reasonable rather than merely dutiful.

Clarke makes the comparison a plain calculation: if the glory that is to be revealed is the enjoyment of God himself, then the sufferings of this life, which when compared with eternity are but as for a moment, are not worthy to be put in competition with this glory which shall be revealed in us, and this case is perfectly clear. On the creature he says there is considerable difficulty in this and the four following verses, and that the difficulty lies chiefly in the meaning of the one word which we translate the creature or the creation. He lists the answers that have been given: some think that by it the brute creation is meant, others apply it to the Jewish people, others to the godly, others to the Gentiles, others to the good angels, and others to the fallen spirits; and he weighs these before settling his own view. Wesley says the verse gives the reason why the apostle had just mentioned sufferings and glory, since when that glory shall be revealed in us the sons of God will be revealed also. On the expectation he says the word denotes a lively hope of something drawing near and a vehement longing after it, and takes the creation to mean all visible creatures, believers excepted, who are spoken of apart, each kind according as it is capable; all these have been sufferers through sin, and to all these, the finally impenitent excepted, shall refreshment redound from the glory of the children of God.
