Barnes says the verse commences a new division of the subject, whose design is to show the power of the gospel in sustaining the soul in trials, a very important and material part of the scheme; this had been partially noticed before, but its full power to support the soul in the prospect of a glorious immortality had not been fully discussed. On the word for earnest expectation he notes that it occurs only here and in the letter to the Philippians, and that it properly denotes a state of earnest desire to see any object when the head is thrust forward, an intense anxiety, an ardent wish, and is thus well employed to denote the intense interest with which a Christian looks to his future inheritance. On the creature he weighs the possible senses at length before settling on the material creation. Ellicott prefers to render the glory as revealed upon us rather than in us, that is reaching to us and illumining and transfiguring us, since the coming of Christ is always conceived of as a visible manifestation of glory in those who take part in it. On the following verse he says that ours is not a merely isolated hope, since the whole creation is looking earnestly and intently for the same manifestation of glory as ourselves; the word for earnest expectation he calls a single word in the Greek and a very striking one, meaning literally a straining forward with outstretched head, just as we might imagine the crowds outside a race-course straining to see what is happening within. Robertson says that we shall be included in the radiance of the coming glory, which will put the present sufferings in the shadow, and notes that precisely the same idiom occurs in the letter to the Galatians. The noun for earnest expectation he says has so far been found nowhere save here and in the letter to the Philippians, though the verb is common in Polybius and Plutarch, and he reports Milligan’s view that Paul may have made the substantive from the verb; it is a double compound formed from the words meaning off from, head, and to watch, hence to watch eagerly with outstretched head.

Theodoret puts the comparison in a series of balances. The crowns exceed the contests; the reward cannot be put in the same scale with the afflictions; small is the affliction, but vast the looked-for gain; and it is for this reason, he says, that the apostle calls the things thus hoped for not payment but glory, since payment would imply a proportion between what is given and what is earned, whereas glory implies none. On the following verse he sets out the widest of all the lists of what waits: perceive ye not, says he, the heaven, the earth, the sea, the air, the sun, the moon, the whole visible creation, and besides these such as are invisible, angels, archangels, powers, dominions, principalities? All these, he concludes, are waiting for your full perfection, so that the believer is not a spectator of the world’s expectancy but its object. Cyril of Jerusalem, whose comment attached here in fact belongs to the later verse about the Spirit’s intercession, explains why the Spirit is called the Comforter: because he comforts and encourages us and helps our infirmities, for we know not what we should pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself makes intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered, that is, makes intercession to God; and he illustrates it from the martyr, outraged and dishonoured unjustly, with tortures on every side and fire and sword.

debates: What is meant by the creature: Clarke says the difficulty of the whole passage lies in this one word and lists six answers that have been given, the brute creation, the Jewish people, the godly, the Gentiles, the good angels and the fallen spirits; Gill reports and questions the view that the universe is meant, since part of the world is afterwards distinguished from it, and mentions the opinion that angels are intended; Wesley confines it to all visible creatures with believers excepted, Calvin extends it to every element and part of the world, and Theodoret to the visible creation together with angels and archangels and principalities

How the connecting particle at the head of the passage should be taken: Calvin denies it can be causal, since nothing precedes for which a reason is given, and proposes that it be read as affirmative or as a particle of transition or addition

Whether the glory is revealed in us or upon us: Ellicott prefers upon us, as reaching to us and transfiguring us, since the coming of Christ is conceived as a visible manifestation of glory in those who share it, and Robertson agrees that we shall be included in its radiance, while Wesley keeps the revealing in us and ties it to the manifestation of the sons of God
outliers: Robertson reports Milligan’s conjecture that the apostle may have coined the noun for earnest expectation from the verb
Ellicott pictures the crowds outside a race-course straining forward with outstretched heads
Theodoret makes the whole visible and invisible creation wait upon the perfecting of the believers
Henry contrasts the sentence of the word with the sentiment of the world on present suffering
themes: the manifestation of the sons of God

20.pericope_label: The creature made subject to vanity in hope: the whole creation groaneth and travaileth together

schools.summary: Gill takes the creature to designate the Gentile world, and explains the vanity as the emptiness of the minds of the Gentiles, who were without God and Christ and the Holy Spirit, without the law and Gospel and grace of God; also the vain conceits they had of themselves, of their wisdom, knowledge, learning and eloquence, and likewise their vain philosophy and particularly their gross idolatry and polytheism. On the hope he corrects the punctuation of the English version: the phrase in hope, which stands at the end of the preceding verse, should be placed at the beginning of this one and read in connection with it, the intervening words being a parenthesis, so that the earnest expectation of the creature waits for the manifestation of the sons of God in hope that the creature itself also shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption. On the groaning he compares a woman with child ready to bring forth, which the following words require. Calvin shows the object of expectation from what is of an opposite character: since creatures, being now subject to corruption, cannot be restored until the sons of God shall be wholly restored, they therefore long for their own renewal and look forward to the manifestation of the celestial kingdom. He explains the vanity as their not abiding in a constant and durable state, and holds that the whole passage teaches how the creation has in hope been made subject to vanity, inasmuch as it shall some time be made free, as Isaiah testifies and Peter confirms still more clearly. From this he draws a sobering inference: it is indeed meet for us to consider what a dreadful curse we have deserved, since all created things, in themselves blameless, both on earth and in the visible heaven, undergo punishment for our sins, so that the ruin visible in nature is a standing testimony against man rather than against nature.

Clarke takes the creature of the Gentile world, and presses a distinction between the two clauses: the Gentile world was subject to vanity of mind, but not willingly, and we may say that it became vain willingly but was made subject to vanity unwillingly. He traces the matter back to the origin of Gentilism, namely the confusion of languages by reason of the attempt to build the tower of Babel, when the nations were dispersed and left to their own devices. On the following verse he connects it closely with the last, reading in hope that the creature itself also shall be delivered, and observes that the word for corruption very frequently denotes sinful corruption, citing the corruption that is through lust, the fear that the minds of readers should be corrupted, and the saying that evil communications corrupt good manners; the deliverance he therefore takes of a moral rather than a merely physical restoration. On the groaning he turns the verse into an argument for his own reading, asking that if it be inquired how the Gentile world groaned and travailed in pain, let them who explain this of the fabric of the material world tell us how that groans and travails; they must needs own it to be a borrowed and allusive phrase, whereas in the sense he has given the very literal construction may be admitted. Wesley glosses the vanity as abuse, misery and corruption, and names the subjector as God, adding that Adam only made the creation liable to the sentence which God pronounced, yet not without hope. On the deliverance he reasons from the word itself: destruction is not deliverance, and therefore whatsoever is destroyed or ceases to be is not delivered at all; will then any part of the creation be destroyed? The glorious liberty he takes as the excellent state wherein they were created, so that the promise is of restoration rather than of annihilation.

Barnes takes the creature here of the renewed creature, the Christian mind, and reads the verse as a reason for its aspiring to the full privileges of adoption, since the present state is not one of choice or one which is preferred, but one to which it has been subjected for wise reasons by God; being subject to vanity means being placed in such a state by the appointment of another. On the following verse he makes the ground of hope the purpose of God that deliverance shall be granted, which sustains the Christian amidst the trials to which he is subjected here, the hope being that this same renewed man shall be delivered from all the toils and cares and sins of this state. On the groaning, however, he parts from his own earlier interpretation, saying that the expression has commonly been understood as meaning the same as the creature in the preceding verses, but that he understands it as having a different signification and as being used in the natural and usual sense of the word creature or creation. Ellicott says the Apostle gives the reason for this earnest expectation in the present state of nature, pointing out what creation is: if creation were perfect, and were fulfilling the noblest possible purpose, there would be no cause for looking forward hopefully to the future; vanity he defines as emptiness or nothingness, creation fulfilling an unworthy instead of a worthy end. On the following verse he gives the reason for the hope which survives through the degradation of nature, namely what creation is to be, and prefers to render the conjunction as that rather than because, joining it to the end of the previous verse so that the sense is in hope that creation also shall be delivered, citing Meyer for this construction; the bondage of corruption he explains as the state of decay and ruin into which the world by nature has fallen, regarded as a servitude. On the groaning he says that in view of the physical evil and misery prevalent in the world the Apostle attributes a human consciousness of pain to the rest of creation, which groans and travails together, that is, every member of it in common with its kind, and that the idea of travailing as in childbirth has reference to the future prospect of joyful delivery. Robertson parses the verb as a second aorist passive, notes that the word for vanity is rare and late though common in the Greek Old Testament and derived from an adjective meaning empty or vain, and says the subjection was not of creation’s own will but was due to the effect of man’s sin, coming by reason of God who subjected it in hope. On the following verse he says it is the hope of creation and not of the Creator, and quotes Godet that nature possesses in the feeling of her unmerited suffering a sort of presentiment of her future deliverance. On the groaning he notes two more compounds formed with the preposition meaning together, both rare and both occurring here alone in the New Testament, and says nature is pictured in the pangs of childbirth. Lightfoot takes the creature of the Gentile world and frames the distinction sharply: the Gentile world was subject to vanity of mind, but not willingly, by reason of him who subjected the same; may we not say that it became vain willingly, but was made subject to vanity not willingly? He recurs for proof to the very first original of Gentilism, that is to the first confusion of languages, and on the following verse he observes that the word for corruption sometimes, indeed very frequently, denotes sinful corruption in the Holy Scriptures, citing corruption through lust, the corrupting of the mind, and the corrupting of good manners by evil communications.

Theodoret identifies the vanity plainly with corruption, since the apostle teaches presently that the creature itself also shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption, and he declares that the whole visible creation had obtained a mortal nature because the Maker of all had foreseen the transgression of man, so that the subjection was not an accident but a provision made in view of what was coming. On the deliverance he sets the two manifestations in their order: when the children of God appear such as they are now called, and in their immortality are manifested to be the sons of God, then the creation also will obtain a total release from corruption, the one waiting upon the other. He then adds the caution that governs his whole reading of the passage: all this the apostle says not meaning that the visible creation really was gifted with feeling or with any power of expectation of its own, but speaking after the manner of men, as prophets often do when they call upon the hills to rejoice or the earth to mourn. The point for Theodoret is that the language is figurative while the doctrine is not, since the corruption laid upon the creation is real and its release will be real, whatever we make of the groaning ascribed to it.

debates: What the creature means in this passage: Gill, Lightfoot and Clarke all take it of the Gentile world, tracing the subjection to the confusion of tongues at Babel and distinguishing a willing vanity of mind from an unwilling subjection; Barnes takes it of the renewed creature, the Christian mind, though at the groaning he abandons that sense for the natural one; while Ellicott, Robertson, Calvin, Wesley and Theodoret take it of the material creation

Whether the groaning of the creation can be read literally: Clarke turns the verse into an argument for his own view, challenging those who explain it of the fabric of the material world to say how that groans and travails, since they must own the phrase borrowed and allusive; Ellicott grants that a human consciousness of pain is attributed to the rest of creation, and Theodoret expressly denies that the visible creation was really gifted with feeling

Where the phrase in hope belongs: Gill places it at the head of the following verse rather than at the close of this one, treating the intervening words as a parenthesis, and Clarke and Ellicott make the same connection, Ellicott preferring to render the conjunction that rather than because on Meyer’s authority
outliers: Wesley argues that destruction is not deliverance, so that whatever ceases to be is not delivered at all
Robertson quotes Godet that nature has in her unmerited suffering a presentiment of her deliverance
Calvin infers the greatness of the curse from the punishment borne by things blameless in themselves
Lightfoot and Clarke both show that the word for corruption commonly denotes moral rather than physical decay

23.pericope_label: We which have the firstfruits of the Spirit groan within ourselves: we are saved by hope

schools.summary: Gill takes the words of the Jews as distinguished from the Gentiles just spoken of, consistently with his reading of the creature in the preceding verses. On the clause about being saved by hope he answers the difficulty from the side of the divine purpose: those who have received the firstfruits, and who were in a lost and perishing condition and by nature no better than others, are saved from sin and from wrath to come by Christ with a spiritual and everlasting salvation; and they were already saved in the preparations and purposes of God, in the covenant of grace, in the arms and hands of Christ through his purchase, so that the hope does not create the salvation but waits for its manifestation. On the closing verse he lists what is hoped for and not seen: the hour of death, the second coming of Christ, the resurrection of the dead, and eternal glory, all of them unseen by us and therefore proper objects of hope. Calvin reports the opinion of those who think the Apostle intended here to exalt the dignity of our future blessedness, and to prove it by this, that all things look for it with ardent desire, not only the irrational parts of creation but we also who have been regenerated by the Spirit of God; and he allows that this view is capable of being defended. But it seems to him rather that there is a comparison here between the greater and the less, as though the apostle argued that if the insensible creation feels the burden, much more must those feel it who have received the firstfruits of the Spirit and know what they are waiting for. On the clause about hope he strengthens the exhortation by another argument, that our salvation cannot be separated from some kind of death, and he proves this by the nature of hope: since hope extends to things not yet obtained, and represents to our minds the form of things hidden and far remote, whatever is either openly seen or really possessed is not an object of hope; and he takes it as granted, and as what cannot be denied, that so long as we are in this world our salvation is hidden and must therefore be waited for.

Clarke takes the words of the Jews, adding the paraphrase that neither the Gentiles only but we Jews also, however we belong to a nation envious of the heathen, to whom God has granted the firstfruits of the Spirit, sigh among ourselves for their sakes, waiting for the adoption, that is the redemption of our mystical body, whereof the Gentiles make a very great part; and he cites the works of an earlier commentator for this construction. On the clause about hope he explains that we are supported and are comfortable in the expectation we have of receiving from the hand of our God all the good we need in the troubles and adversities of this life, and of having our bodies raised from corruption and death at the general resurrection; and since hope signifies the expectation of future good, it necessarily supposes that the object of it is not yet possessed. On the closing verse he says that if we have a well-grounded expectation of our resurrection and final glorification, knowing that such things are necessarily future and must for a certain time be delayed, then we patiently wait for them and continue patiently to endure the common ills of life and whatever tribulations we may be exposed to in consequence of our Christian profession, for we know that faithful is he who has promised. Wesley identifies the firstfruits with the Spirit himself, who is the firstfruits of our inheritance, and explains the adoption from a Roman custom: persons who had been privately adopted among the Romans were often brought forth into the forum and there publicly owned as their sons by those who adopted them, and so at the general resurrection, when the body itself is redeemed from death, the sons of God shall be publicly owned by him before all creation. On the clause about hope he says our salvation is now only in hope and that we do not yet possess this full salvation.

Barnes takes the words of Christians as distinguished from the creation in general, and explains the firstfruits from the harvest: the word properly denotes the portion first collected and consecrated to God as an offering of gratitude, and hence means that which is first in order of time, so that the gift of the Spirit is the earnest of what follows. On the clause about hope he denies at the outset that hope can be the instrument or condition of salvation, and reports that most commentators have understood the words as meaning that we have as yet attained salvation only in hope, that we have arrived only at a condition in which we hope for future glory, and that we are in an attitude of waiting for the future state of adoption; but he suggests that the word saved may here mean simply that we are kept or preserved. On the closing verse he states the psychology of patience: the effect described exists everywhere, for where there is a strong desire for an object and a corresponding expectation of obtaining it, which together constitute true hope, then we can wait for it with patience, whereas where there is a strong desire without a corresponding expectation there is impatience; and as the Christian has a strong desire of future glory together with an expectation of obtaining it, he can wait. Ellicott says it is not only the rest of creation that groans, for we Christians too, though we possess the firstfruits of the Spirit, nevertheless inwardly groan, sighing for the time when our adoption as the sons of God will be complete and even our mortal bodies will be transfigured; the firstfruits he explains as the first partial outpouring of the Spirit as opposed to the plenitude of glory. On the clause about hope he asks why the apostle says we wait for the adoption, and answers that hope in the future is of the very essence of the Christian’s life, since it was by hope that he was saved and hope at the time when he first believed made him realise his salvation though it is still future; this is implied in the very nature of hope, whose proper object is that which is future and unseen. He remarks that it is usually faith rather than hope that is spoken of as the means of salvation. On the closing verse he draws the plain consequence: if salvation were something that could be seen and grasped by sight there would be no room for hope, but as it is we do not see it, we do hope for it, and therefore we patiently endure the sufferings that lie upon the road to it. Robertson calls the firstfruits an old and common metaphor and takes the following genitive as one of apposition, tracing the gift from the great Pentecost through the gifts described in the first letter to the Corinthians and the moral and spiritual fruits named in the letter to the Galatians, and adding that greater ones are still to come; the repeated pronoun he takes as emphatic, and the groaning as our own. On the clause about hope he parses the first aorist passive of the verb to save and notes that the case of the noun for hope is not certain, the form being the same for locative, instrumental and dative; curiously enough, he says, either makes good sense in this context, so that we were saved in hope, by hope, for hope, namely the hope of the redemption of the body.

Theodoret turns the comparison of the two groanings into an argument. And what wonder, he asks, if creation is so affected on our account, when even ourselves, who have already received many pledges of the future and above all others the grace of the Spirit, groan in our longings after freedom? The pledge already given, on his reading, does not remove the longing but sharpens it, since a man who has tasted something of what is coming feels the delay more and not less than one who has tasted nothing. What is waited for he defines exactly from the words that follow, the adoption, to wit the redemption of the body, so that the sonship already conferred is not complete while the body remains mortal. On the clause about hope he says that not yet have we attained unto the resurrection, but having received the promise we are comforted by our hopes; and he repeats the apostle’s own definition with approval, that hope which is seen is not hope, for what a man sees, how does he yet hope for it? The comfort he describes is therefore not a present possession of the thing but a present certainty about it, which is precisely what makes the groaning compatible with the joy.

debates: What being saved by hope means: Barnes denies that hope can be the instrument or condition of salvation, reports the common view that we have attained salvation only in hope, and proposes instead that saved may here mean kept or preserved; Robertson finds the case of the noun undetermined between locative, instrumental and dative, and observes that we were saved in hope, by hope and for hope all make good sense; Ellicott notes that it is usually faith rather than hope that is named as the means of salvation, and Gill answers from the divine purpose that the salvation was already secured in the covenant and in the hands of Christ

Who the ourselves are that groan: Gill and Clarke take them of the Jews as distinguished from the Gentile creature of the preceding verses, Clarke adding that they sigh for the Gentiles’ sake, while Barnes and Ellicott take them simply of Christians as distinguished from the creation at large

Why the apostle appeals to the groaning of the creation at all: Calvin reports the view that it exalts the dignity of the future blessedness by showing that all things desire it, allows that this can be defended, but prefers an argument from the less to the greater, and Theodoret presses the same comparison, that those who have received the firstfruits feel the delay more sharply and not less
outliers: Wesley explains the adoption from the Roman practice of bringing a privately adopted son into the forum to be publicly owned
Barnes derives the firstfruits from the portion of harvest first gathered and consecrated
Barnes distinguishes true hope, which joins desire to expectation and so can wait, from desire without expectation, which produces impatience
Clarke includes among the things patiently waited for the common ills of life and the tribulations of the Christian profession

26.pericope_label: The Spirit helpeth our infirmities and maketh intercession with groanings which cannot be uttered

schools.summary: Gill sets the help of the Spirit among his other offices already named in the chapter: it is the Spirit of God who dwells in us, by whom we are led, who is the spirit of adoption to us, who has witnessed to our spirits that we are the children of God, and whose firstfruits we have received; over and above all this he also helps our infirmities while we are groaning within ourselves. On the searching of the hearts he says this is peculiar to God and is a periphrasis of him, since angels, neither good nor bad, can search into the hearts of men, one man cannot know the heart of another, nor can any man fully know his own; this is the prerogative of God alone. Calvin explains why the help is brought in at this point: that the faithful may not make the objection that they are so weak as not to be able to bear so many and so heavy burdens, the apostle brings before them the aid of the Spirit, which is abundantly sufficient to overcome all difficulties; there is then no reason for any one to complain that the bearing of the cross is beyond his own strength, since we are sustained by a celestial power. On the following verse he calls it a remarkable reason for strengthening our confidence, that we are heard by God when we pray through his Spirit, for he thoroughly knows our desires even as he knows the thoughts of his own Spirit. He notices particularly the suitableness of the phrase about the will of God, since it intimates that God does not regard these emotions of the Spirit as new and strange, nor reject them as unreasonable, but allows and approves them as his own work; and from this he draws the assurance that prayers so prompted cannot fail of a hearing, however inarticulate they may be.

Henry suggests two further privileges to which true Christians are entitled, of which the first is the help of the Spirit in prayer. While we are in this world, he says, hoping and waiting for what we see not, we must be praying, since hope supposes desire and that desire offered up to God is prayer, and so we groan. He then sets out our weakness in prayer under two heads: as to the matter of our prayers we know not what we should pray for, being often ignorant of what is really good for us and apt to ask for what would hurt us, and as to the manner we know not how to pray as we ought, our best duties needing to be pardoned. Against this weakness he sets the office of the Spirit, who helps by suggesting what to ask and by working in us the desires that are agreeable to the will of God, so that the prayer which the Christian cannot frame is nevertheless framed within him. The groanings which cannot be uttered Henry takes not as a defect but as an evidence, since the strength of the desire is what makes it inexpressible, and he draws the comfort that such prayers are the most likely to be heard because they are the least of our own making. He adds that the searcher of hearts needs no words, so that the weakest believer is not at a disadvantage before him.

Clarke insists on the identity of the Spirit here with the one mentioned before as bearing witness with ours that we are the children of God, and draws a firm conclusion from it: consequently it is not a disposition or frame of mind, for the disposition of our mind surely cannot help the infirmities of our minds. On the verb he says the word is very inadequately expressed by helpeth, being compounded of the preposition meaning together and another meaning over against, so that it describes taking hold of a burden at the opposite end and bearing it along with another, as two men carry a weight between them. On the following verse he explains that the verb rendered maketh intercession signifies to apply oneself to a person on behalf of another, to intercede or negotiate for; our Lord makes intercession for us by negotiating and managing, as our friend and agent, all the affairs pertaining to our salvation, while the Spirit of God makes intercession for the saints not by supplication to God on their behalf but by directing and qualifying their own supplications, so that the two intercessions are of different kinds. Wesley finds a boldness in the language which he does not soften: not only the universe, not only the children of God, but the Spirit of God also himself, as it were, groaneth, while he helpeth our infirmities or weaknesses. He enumerates those weaknesses: our understandings are weak, particularly in the things of God; our desires are weak; our prayers are weak; we know not many times what we should pray for, and much less are we able to pray for it as we ought. On the following verse he says that he who searches the hearts, wherein the Spirit dwells and intercedes, knows what is the mind of the Spirit though man cannot utter it, and that the intercession is made for the saints, who are near to God, according to his will, as is worthy of God and acceptable to him.

Barnes says the verse introduces a new source of consolation and support, that which is derived from the Spirit, and continues the argument to show the sustaining power of the Christian religion; the Spirit here undoubtedly refers to the Holy Spirit who dwells in us and strengthens us, and the word rendered helpeth properly means to sustain with us, to aid us in supporting a burden. On the following verse he says that to search the heart is one of God’s attributes which cannot be communicated to a creature, and that he knows the desires which the Holy Spirit excites and produces in the heart; God does not need that these deep emotions should be expressed in words, nor does he need the eloquence of language to induce him to hear, but he sees the desire itself. Ellicott marks the balance of the argument: while on the one hand the prospect of salvation sustains the Christian, on the other the Divine Spirit interposes to aid him, the one source of encouragement being human, namely his own consciousness of the certainty of salvation, and the other divine. He notes that the correct reading of the noun is the singular, infirmity, and that without this assistance we might be too weak to endure. On the following verse he says God recognises the voice of his own Spirit because the prayers that the Spirit prompts are in strict accordance with his will, and explains the phrase about the mind of the Spirit as meaning the thoughts of the Spirit, and therefore the echo of those thoughts in the prayers that are offered. Robertson parses the verb as a present middle indicative of a late and striking double compound found in Diodorus, in the Greek Old Testament and in Josephus, and frequent in the inscriptions according to Deissmann, meaning to lend a hand together with, at the same time with, another; it occurs only twice in the New Testament, here and in Martha’s plea for Mary’s help, and here, he says, the apostle beautifully pictures the Holy Spirit taking hold at our side. On the following verse he identifies the searcher as God, compares the phrase rendered according to the will of God with its use in the second letter to the Corinthians, and observes that the Holy Spirit is the other Paraclete who pleads God’s cause with us as Christ is our Paraclete with the Father; but more is true here, for the Holy Spirit also interprets our prayers to God and makes intercession for us.

Theodoret takes the assistance of the Spirit as sufficient in itself, since we know not what we should pray for as we ought, and draws from the verse a rule of practice rather than a doctrine: ask not, says he, to be delivered from affliction, for you know not what is profitable to you as does God your Governor; resign yourselves into his hands. On the following verse he states his interpretation without hedging: by the Spirit here the apostle means not the Holy Ghost himself, but the grace given to the faithful; for stirred up by this we pray the more earnestly, and with sighings inexpressible by words implore God our Saviour. He adds that the holy apostle writes this from what he had himself experienced, so that the description of inarticulate groaning is drawn from a man who had prayed in that way and not from speculation. Cyril of Jerusalem uses the same verse to explain one of the titles of the Spirit: he is called the Comforter because he comforts and encourages us and helps our infirmities, for we know not what we should pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself makes intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered, that is, makes intercession to God. He illustrates the need from the case of the martyr: oftentimes a man for Christ’s sake has been outraged and dishonoured unjustly, martyrdom is at hand, tortures on every side, and fire and sword, and in such straits it is the Comforter who stands by.

debates: Whether the Spirit that intercedes is the Holy Ghost himself or the grace given to believers: Theodoret says expressly that the apostle means not the Holy Ghost himself but the grace given to the faithful, by which we are stirred up to pray the more earnestly, whereas Clarke argues the contrary from the identity with the Spirit who bears witness, since a disposition of our own mind could not help the infirmities of our minds, and Barnes, Robertson and Calvin all take it of the Holy Spirit

What sort of intercession is meant: Clarke distinguishes two kinds, our Lord interceding by negotiating and managing our affairs as friend and agent, and the Spirit interceding not by supplication to God on our behalf but by directing and qualifying our own petitions, while Robertson sets the two Paracletes side by side and adds that the Spirit also interprets our prayers to God

What our ignorance in prayer consists in: Henry divides it into the matter and the manner, since we neither know what to ask nor how to ask it, Wesley enumerates weak understandings, weak desires and weak prayers, and Theodoret turns the ignorance into a rule, that we should not ask to be delivered from affliction since we do not know what is profitable for us
outliers: Clarke and Robertson both press the compound verb, which pictures one taking hold of a burden at the opposite end and lifting along with us
Robertson finds the same verb only once more in the New Testament, in Martha’s complaint that Mary would not lend a hand
Ellicott notes that the true reading of the noun is the singular, infirmity
Cyril of Jerusalem illustrates the need of the Comforter from the martyr facing fire and sword

28.pericope_label: All things work together for good: whom he foreknew, predestinated, called, justified, glorified

schools.summary: Gill distinguishes three goods that may be intended, a temporal, a spiritual and an eternal one. Temporal good is what the men of the world are seeking after and generally have the greatest share of, while the saints have the least; yet they have as much as is needful for them, and what they have they have with a blessing, and even afflictions sometimes work for their temporal good. On the foreknowledge he denies that the prescience of all things future is here intended, by which God foreknows and foretells things to come and is distinguished from all other gods, and which is so called not with respect to himself, with whom all things are present, but with respect to us; the foreknowledge here is rather a knowledge of love and approbation, fixed on particular persons. On the predestination he observes that it is not to sufferings, which are neither expressed nor designed, but to grace and to the glory afterwards mentioned; that it is of particular persons, who in consequence of it are called and justified and glorified; that it is the effect of divine grace and entirely owing to it; and that it is the source of all the other blessings of grace, and is therefore placed at the head of them. Calvin draws the conclusion from what had been said, that so far are the troubles of this life from hindering our salvation that on the contrary they are helps to it; and he notices the illative particle, observing that it is no new thing with the apostle to make a somewhat indiscriminate use of adverbs, and that this conclusion also anticipates an objection, since the judgment of the flesh would say otherwise. On the foreknowledge and the conformity he shows by the very order of election that the afflictions of the faithful are nothing else than the manner by which they are conformed to the image of Christ, and that this was necessary he had already declared; there is therefore no reason for us to be grieved, or to think it hard and grievous that we are afflicted, unless we would disapprove of the Lord’s election itself, by which we have been foreordained to this very conformity. The comfort he draws is that the cross is not an interruption of the purpose but a part of its execution.

Henry defines the good narrowly and practically: that is good for the saints which does their souls good. Every providence tends to the spiritual good of those that love God, in breaking them off from sin, bringing them nearer to God, weaning them from the world, and fitting them for heaven; and when the saints act out of character, corrections will be employed to bring them back again. He then turns to the verses that follow and calls what they contain the order of the causes of our salvation, a golden chain, in which every link holds and none can be broken. He observes that the apostle, having reckoned up so many ingredients of the happiness of true believers, comes here to represent the ground of them all, which he lays in predestination: these precious privileges are conveyed to us by the charter of the covenant, but they are founded in the counsel of God, which infallibly secures the event, so that Jesus Christ the purchaser might not labour in vain nor spend his strength for nought. Henry takes the certainty of the chain as the ground of the believer’s comfort rather than a matter for speculation, since what is secured in the counsel of God cannot be defeated by anything the believer meets with in the way; and he presses that the conformity to the image of the Son, which stands in the middle of the chain, is the end for which the afflictions already described are permitted.

Clarke lays down cautions for reading the verse rightly. First, the persons in whose behalf all things work for good are they who love God and consequently live in the spirit of obedience. Second, it is not said that all things shall work for good, but that they work now, in the present, on behalf of him who loves now; so that the promise is not a general prediction about the future but a description of what is presently true of a particular character. On the foreknowledge he takes the two verses as showing how our calling is an argument that all things work together to advance our eternal happiness, by setting out the several steps which the wisdom and goodness of God have settled in order to complete our salvation, giving first the foundation and the finishing, or the beginning and the end. On the chain of verbs he reads the whole of the Gentiles, whom God determined to call into his Church along with the Jewish people, and whom he invited by the preaching of the Gospel to believe on his Son; and he observes that it is worthy of note that all that is spoken here refers to what had already taken place, since the calling, the justifying and the glorifying are represented as having already occurred. Wesley says we know this in general, though we do not always know particularly what to pray for, and enumerates what the all things covers: ease or pain, poverty or riches, and the ten thousand changes of life, all working strongly and sweetly for spiritual and eternal good. The calling according to his purpose he explains as God’s gracious design of saving a lost world by the death of his Son. On the foreknowledge he finds the answer within the verse itself: the apostle declares who those are whom he foreknew and predestinated to glory, namely those who are conformable to the image of his Son, and this conformity is the mark of those who are foreknown and who will be glorified.

Barnes says the verse introduces another source of consolation and support, drawn from the fact that all things are under the direction of an infinitely wise Being who has purposed the salvation of the Christian and has so appointed all things that they shall contribute to it; the all things include all our afflictions and trials and all the persecutions and calamities to which we are exposed. On the foreknowledge he reports that the word has been the subject of almost endless disputes in regard to its meaning in this place, granting that its literal meaning cannot be a matter of dispute, since it denotes properly to know beforehand or to be acquainted with future events, but that whether it means here simply to know that certain persons would become Christians, or to ordain and constitute them such, is the point at issue. On the chain he says the apostle states the connexion between predestination and certain salvation in order to show Christians the true consolation to be derived from it, since the one implied the other, and takes the calling as a calling by the Spirit to become Christians and not merely an outward invitation. Ellicott reports a rather remarkable reading of the first verse found in the Vatican and Alexandrian manuscripts and in Origen, which inserts God as the subject of the verb and makes all things the object, so that God works all things with us or co-operates in all things; this reading, he judges, is very early if not original. On the predestination he admits that this is the term which seems most to interfere with human free-will, and distinguishes it carefully from foreknowledge: foreknowledge does not interfere with free-will, because the foreknowledge, though prior in point of time, is posterior in the order of causation to the act of choice, since a man does not choose a certain action because it is foreknown, but it is foreknown because he will choose it. Robertson notes that two of the chief manuscripts supply God as the subject of the verb in the first verse, and says that this is the idea in any case, since it is God who makes all things work together in our lives for an ultimate good. On the foreknowledge he parses the second aorist active of an old verb and the first aorist of a late verb meaning to appoint beforehand, another compound formed with the preposition meaning before, and observes that this foreknowledge and choice is placed in eternity in the letter to the Ephesians. On the chain he parses the three verbs as first aorist active indicatives of common verbs, and notes that the glorification is stated as already consummated, all of them being constative aorists, though it is still in the future in the fullest sense; he quotes Sanday and Headlam that the step implied in the last verb is both complete and certain in the divine counsels.

Chrysostom reads the whole surrounding argument as addressed to men in danger. Here, he says, the apostle seems to have mooted this whole topic with a view to those who were in peril, and not this only but also what was said a little before: the words that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us, and those that the whole creation groaneth, and the saying that we are saved by hope, were all directed to the same readers under the same pressure. The effect for him is that the doctrine is pastoral before it is speculative, and that the promise about all things working together is offered as a support to men actually suffering rather than as a general maxim. Theodoret restricts the promise carefully. They work not together with all, he says, but with those that love him, nor simply work with them, but work with them for good; and he presses the qualification into a rule about prayer, that if any ask for what would not be profitable to him he fails of his petition, because it is to his advantage not to gain it. The failure of a prayer is thus itself an instance of the all things working for good, which is exactly the comfort the verse is meant to give. Cyril of Jerusalem gives the conformity to the image a sacramental ground: having been baptized into Christ and put on Christ, the newly baptized have been made conformable to the Son of God, since God, having foreordained us unto adoption as sons, made us to be conformed to the body of Christ’s glory; and having become partakers of Christ they are properly called anointed, of whom God said, Touch not my anointed.

debates: Whether God is the subject of the verb in the first verse: Ellicott reports a remarkable reading found in the Vatican and Alexandrian manuscripts and in Origen which inserts God as subject and makes all things the object, and judges it very early if not original, while Robertson notes the same two manuscripts and says the idea is the same in any case

What foreknew means: Barnes reports almost endless disputes and sets out the alternatives, simply knowing that certain persons would become Christians or ordaining and constituting them such; Gill excludes the bare prescience of all things future; Ellicott defends free-will by arguing that foreknowledge, though prior in time, is posterior in the order of causation to the act of choice; and Wesley finds the answer within the verse, that those foreknown are the very ones conformable to the image of the Son

How the past tense of glorified is to be taken: Robertson calls the verbs constative aorists and says the glorification is stated as already consummated though still future in the fullest sense, quoting Sanday and Headlam that the step is complete and certain in the divine counsels, while Clarke takes all the verbs as referring to what had already taken place and reads the whole of the calling of the Gentiles
outliers: Henry calls the sequence of verbs the order of the causes of our salvation, a golden chain
Theodoret turns the failure of a prayer into an instance of all things working for good
Chrysostom reads the whole passage as addressed to men actually in danger rather than as a general maxim
Cyril of Jerusalem grounds the conformity to the image on baptism, and calls the baptized anointed

31.pericope_label: If God be for us, who can be against us: he that spared not his own Son

schools.summary: Gill leaves the reference of these things open, allowing two possibilities. It may be to the afflictions just spoken of, and then the question is whether we shall murmur and repine at them; and the answer is no, since they work together for our good and are not to be compared with our future glory, which is certain, for if we suffer with and for Christ we shall be glorified together. Or it may be to the blessings just mentioned, the foreknowledge of God, divine predestination, effectual calling, free justification and eternal glorification, and then the question is what use we shall make of them. On the sparing he draws up a list of what God did not spare in order to set the wonder in relief: it is said that God spared not the angels that sinned, nor the old world which was full of violence, nor Sodom and Gomorrah whose wickedness was great, nor the Egyptians and their firstborn who refused to let Israel go, nor the Israelites themselves when they transgressed his laws, nor wicked men hardened in sin; all which is not to be wondered at. But that he should not spare his own Son is another matter altogether, and it is here that the argument of the verse rests. Calvin says the subject discussed having been sufficiently proved, the apostle now breaks out into exclamations, by which he sets forth the magnanimity with which the faithful ought to be furnished when adversities urge them to despond; and he teaches us in these words that with the paternal favour of God is connected that invincible courage which overcomes all temptations. We indeed know, he adds, that judgment is usually formed of the love or the hatred of God from the outward appearance of things, so that men conclude God to be against them when things go hard with them; against which the apostle sets a favour known otherwise than by circumstances. On the following verse he says that as it greatly concerns us to be so thoroughly persuaded of the paternal love of God as to be able to retain our rejoicing on its account, Paul brings forward the price of our redemption in order to prove that God favours us; and doubtless it is a remarkable and clear evidence of inappreciable love that the Father refused not to bestow his Son for our salvation. From this he draws an argument from the greater to the less, that having given what is greatest God will not withhold what is smaller.

Henry says the apostle closes this excellent discourse upon the privileges of believers with a holy triumph in the name of all the saints. Having largely set forth the mystery of God’s love to us in Christ, and the exceedingly great and precious privileges we enjoy by him, he concludes like an orator, asking what we shall then say to these things and what use we shall make of all that has been said; and he speaks, Henry observes, as one amazed and swallowed up with the greatness of the subject. On the following verse he says that all things whatever, in heaven and earth, are not so great a display of God’s free love as the gift of his coequal Son to be the atonement on the cross for the sin of man, and that all the rest follows upon union with him and interest in him. The all things he defines as all which can be the causes or means of any real good to the faithful Christian, and he draws the practical inference in a sentence: he that has prepared a crown and a kingdom for us will give us what we need in the way to it. The argument as Henry states it is not that the believer will receive whatever he wishes, but that the greater gift already made is the security for every lesser one that is genuinely needed, so that the promise is a ground of confidence rather than of presumption.

Clarke asks what conclusion should be drawn from the premises laid down, not only in the preceding chapters but especially in the verses immediately before, and answers as if the apostle had said: what comfort may we derive from these doctrines? God has called us all to holiness, and to love to him, which is the principle of holiness; we are persecuted and despised, it is true, but the doctrines already established are our sufficient answer. On the following verse he turns the argument into a question about lesser blessings: can we, his sincere followers, doubt of the safety of our state or the certainty of his protection? No; for if he loved us, Gentiles and Jews, so intensely as to deliver up to death his own Son for us all, can he withhold from us any minor blessing? Nay, will he not on the contrary freely give us all things? And he recalls what was said to Abraham, who is the father of the faithful and the representative of them all, as confirming the same reasoning. Wesley counts the structure of the passage precisely: here follow four periods, one general and three particular, each beginning with glorying in the grace of God, which is followed by a question suitable to it, challenging all opponents, to all which the declaration that he is persuaded serves as a general answer. He adds that when the apostle asks what we shall say to these things, related in the third and fifth and eighth chapters, it is as if he had said that we cannot go, think, or wish anything farther. On the following verse he divides it into four sentences: he spared not his own Son, therefore he will freely give us all things; he delivered him up for us all, therefore none can lay anything to our charge. The word freely he explains as marking that all which follows justification is a free gift also, and the all things as whatever is needful or profitable for us.

Barnes asks what fairly follows from the facts stated, or what conclusion should be drawn in regard to the power of the Christian religion to support us in our trials from the considerations already advanced, and proceeds to state the influence. God being for us means that he is on our side or is our friend, as he has shown himself to be by adopting us and by granting to us his Spirit and by the other benefits already enumerated in the chapter. On the following verse he explains the sparing as not retaining or keeping his Son from suffering and death, and says this gave the highest proof of love that a father could give and the highest demonstration of his willingness to do good to those for whom he gave him; the delivering up he takes as giving him into the hands of men and to a cruel death, and the words for us all as meaning for all Christians, since the connexion requires that the expression be so understood. Robertson traces the argument from earlier in the chapter, saying that the apostle has made a triumphant presentation of the reasons for the certainty of the final sanctification of the sons of God and has reached the climax with the word glorified; but he observes that Paul now lets the objector have his say, as he usually does, so that in the remaining verses of the chapter he considers the objections one by one, the first of them being met by this question. On the following verse he notes the intensive particle, which magnifies the deed and may be rendered who as much as this, and parses the first aorist middle of an old verb which is used in the Greek Old Testament about the offering of Isaac. The gift of his own Son, he adds, is the promise and the pledge of the all things working for good spoken of earlier in the chapter, since Christ is all and carries all with him.

Theodoret presses the sweep of the challenge rather than its comfort. Having God as our ally, he asks, shall we be afraid of men? And he observes that the apostle comprehends all things at once under the single word who, whether kings, or generals, or peoples, or their leaders, the whole world at once; the question is deliberately left unqualified so that no adversary can be imagined outside it. Then, he says, the apostle brings forward the crowning blessing of blessings. On the following verse he puts the argument in two questions: he has given us the greater, and shall he not give also the less? his own Son has he bestowed, and will he deprive us of what we have gained? The reasoning is thus not that we deserve the lesser gifts but that the greater one has already settled the question of God’s disposition toward us. Theodoret then adds a christological caution which he thinks the verse requires: here we must remember that the Person of the Son is but one, for it was the human nature that was delivered up on our behalf, and it was delivered up by the divinity; and he supports the distinction from the language used of the bread in the words of institution, so that what is said of the one nature is rightly predicated of the single Person.

debates: What these things refers to: Gill allows either the afflictions just spoken of, in which case the question is whether we shall murmur at them, or the blessings just enumerated, the foreknowledge, predestination, calling, justification and glorification, in which case the question is what use we shall make of them; Barnes and Clarke both take it of the whole preceding argument and ask what comfort follows from it

How the closing verses stand to what precedes: Robertson holds that the apostle, having reached his climax at glorified, now deliberately lets the objector have his say and answers the objections one by one, while Henry treats the passage as a holy triumph and a rhetorical conclusion, and Wesley counts four periods, one general and three particular, each a glorying followed by a challenge

What the all things freely given covers: Henry restricts it to all which can be the causes or means of any real good to the faithful Christian, Wesley to whatever is needful or profitable, and Robertson makes the gift of the Son the pledge of the all things working for good named earlier, while Theodoret argues simply from the greater to the less
outliers: Gill lists what God did not spare, the sinning angels, the old world, Sodom, the Egyptians and Israel itself, to set the sparing of the Son in relief
Robertson notes that the verb for sparing is the one used of the offering of Isaac
Theodoret adds a christological caution, that the human nature was delivered up by the divinity and the Person of the Son is one
Calvin observes that men usually judge God’s love or hatred from the outward appearance of things

33.pericope_label: Who shall lay anything to the charge of God’s elect: it is Christ that died, yea rather that is risen again

schools.summary: Gill defines the elect of God as a certain select number of persons whom he has so loved as, of his sovereign good will and pleasure, to choose in Christ before the foundation of the world unto eternal life and salvation, by certain ways and means of his own appointing, such as sanctification and faith, so that they are peculiarly his. He then faces the obvious objection: are these persons chargeable with nothing criminal? and answers that they are indeed chargeable with Adam’s sin, with a want of original righteousness and with much besides, so that the security does not lie in their innocence but in the justification that follows. On the condemning he says that all mankind are deserving of condemnation and are under its sentence as in Adam, that some are foreordained to condemnation, that all in final impenitence and unbelief are condemned already, and that the whole world of the ungodly will be condemned at the last day; but none of God’s elect are or shall be condemned, for they are loved with an everlasting love, they are chosen unto salvation, and they are in Christ, where there is no condemnation. Calvin makes the persuasion of God’s fatherly kindness the foundation of the whole passage: the first and chief consolation of the godly in adversities is to be fully persuaded of the paternal kindness of God, for hence arises the certainty of their salvation and that calm quietness of the soul through which it comes that adversities are sweetened, or at least the bitterness of sorrow mitigated; hardly then could a more suitable encouragement to patience be adduced than this, a conviction that God is propitious to us, and hence the apostle makes this confidence the main thing. On the condemning he states the legal principle without ornament: as no one by accusing can prevail when the judge absolves, so there remains no condemnation when satisfaction is given to the laws and the penalty is already paid. Christ is he who, having once for all suffered the punishment due to us, thereby declared that he undertook our cause in order to deliver us; and he then who seeks hereafter to condemn us must bring back Christ himself to death again. But he has not only died, Calvin adds, but also came forth by a resurrection as the conqueror of death, so that the ground of the security is doubled.

Clarke observes that this and the two following verses contain a string of questions, most appropriately introduced and most powerfully urged, tending to show the safety of the state of those who have believed the Gospel of the grace of God; and he lays the verses down as they are pointed by the best Greek critics, so that the answers themselves are put interrogatively: who shall lay anything to the charge of God’s elect, God who justifieth? who is he that condemneth, Christ who died, or rather who is risen again? He explains the session at the right hand as the exaltation of our human nature, which the Son took into conjunction with his divinity, and the intercession as his managing all the concerns of his own kingdom in general and of every member of his Church in particular. Wesley, citing an author he has used before, gives a historical account of the term elect: long before the coming of Christ the heathen world revolted from the true God and were therefore reprobated or rejected, while the nation of the Jews was chosen to be the people of God and was therefore styled the children or sons of God, a holy people, a chosen seed, the elect, and the called of God, and these titles were given to all the nation and not to a select portion of it. On the following verse he says our faith should not stop at Christ’s death but be exercised farther on his resurrection, his kingdom and his second coming, and explains the intercession as his presenting there his obedience, his sufferings, his prayers, and our prayers sanctified through him.

Barnes notes that the expression is taken from courts of law and means, who shall accuse or condemn or so charge with crime before the tribunal of God as to cause their condemnation. God’s elect he takes as his chosen people, those chosen according to his eternal purpose; as they are the chosen of God they are dear to him, and as he purposed to save them he will do it in such a way that none can bring against them a charge that will condemn them. On the following verse he asks who shall pass sentence of condemnation and consign to perdition, observes that the office of passing such sentence belongs to Christ, the Judge of quick and dead, and says the apostle proceeds to show that it is certain he will not condemn the elect of God, so that they are secure. The clause about Christ’s death he suggests may be rendered as a question, whether Christ who has died shall condemn them, the argument being that since he died to save them he will not now condemn them. Ellicott connects the remainder of the verse closely with the opening of the next, so that the sense runs that he who died and rose is Christ, and then, who shall separate us from his love; the two questions, who is he that condemneth and who shall separate us, are really parts of the reply to the main question thrown into an interrogative form, and at another moment the sentence would probably have been differently cast, but the Apostle’s mind is in an attitude of challenge. Robertson parses the future active of an old verb meaning to come forward as accuser in a case in court, a forensic term meaning to impeach, and notes that its only New Testament examples are in the Acts; Satan, he observes, is the great Accuser of the brethren, while God is the Judge who sets us right according to his plan for justification, so that the Accuser must face the Judge with his charge. On the following verse he notes that the participle may be either present or future, condemns or shall condemn, and remarks that it is a bold accuser who can face God with false charges, or with true ones for that matter, since we have an Advocate at God’s court who is at the right hand of God and who also makes intercession for us; our Advocate paid the debt for our sins with his blood, so that the score is settled.

Theodoret sets the two questions in their sequence and treats the second as following necessarily from the first. Having said that while God helps no one can injure us, the apostle adds that God, having rendered us justified, leaves no one who can condemn; the justification is thus not merely a benefit alongside the divine help but the answer to a distinct threat, the accusation rather than the assault. On the clauses that follow he asks what more than all this can be sought: in our behalf the Lord Christ died, and having risen again sits by the Father; nor even thus has he ceased his care for us, but pointing to the firstfruits which he took from us he intercedes on our behalf. The accumulation is the argument, since each clause removes a fresh ground of fear, and the last removes the fear that what was done once has been left behind. Cyril of Jerusalem, on the session at the right hand, gathers a series of testimonies: the words in the Gospel according to Matthew that henceforth ye shall see the Son of Man sitting on the right hand of power, the statement of the Apostle Peter that Jesus Christ is on the right hand of God, having gone into heaven, and the words of the Apostle Paul in this very place; and he adds others of the same kind, so that the doctrine may be seen to rest not on a single text but on the consent of the Gospels and the apostles together.

debates: How the verses should be pointed: Clarke lays them down as pointed by the best Greek critics, so that the answers are themselves questions, who shall lay anything to the charge of God’s elect, God who justifieth, and who is he that condemneth, Christ who died; while Ellicott makes a different join, carrying the remainder of the verse forward into the next so that he who died and rose is Christ, and the question who shall separate us follows immediately, the whole being a reply thrown into interrogative form because the Apostle’s mind is in an attitude of challenge

Who the elect are: Gill takes them as a certain select number chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world by sovereign good pleasure, and grants that they are chargeable with Adam’s sin and much besides, so that their security rests on justification and not innocence; Wesley cites an author for a national and historical sense, that the heathen world was rejected while the whole Jewish nation was chosen and styled the elect and the called of God; Barnes takes them simply as those chosen according to God’s eternal purpose

Whether the clause about Christ’s death is a statement or a question: Barnes suggests it may be rendered as asking whether Christ, who has died, shall condemn them, and argues that since he died to save them he will not, while Robertson notes that the participle for condemning may be read either as present or as future
outliers: Robertson names Satan the great Accuser who must face the Judge with his charge, and calls Christ our Advocate who has settled the score
Calvin argues that whoever would condemn us must first bring Christ back to death again
Cyril of Jerusalem gathers testimonies to the session at the right hand from Matthew, from Peter and from Paul
Clarke explains the session as the exaltation of the human nature the Son took into conjunction with his divinity
themes: the session at God’s right hand

35.pericope_label: Who shall separate us from the love of Christ: nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors

schools.summary: Gill insists that by the love of Christ is not meant the saints’ love to Christ but his love to them; he is indeed the object of their love, and so strong is their love to him that it can never be destroyed, for though there may be an abatement in its fervour it can never be lost, yet this is not what is intended here, since the security of the believer must rest on the stronger love and not the weaker. On the quotation he says the passage is cited out of the psalm and means that for the sake of God and his pure worship the Old Testament saints were frequently put to death or exposed to persecutions which often issued in death, as New Testament saints have been for the sake of Christ and his Gospel. On the answer he notes that the intervening words are a parenthesis, so that what follows is the direct answer to the question whether tribulation shall separate us, and the answer is that it shall not, nor any of the other things mentioned; and in all these things, afflictions and distresses and persecutions and famine and nakedness and sword, believers are more than conquerors. On the persuasion he says these words express the strong persuasion and full assurance of faith which the apostle had, that nothing whatever could separate him and the rest of God’s people from God’s love toward them in Christ Jesus; and he adds two observations, that this persuasion regards not himself only but others also, and that it is not conjectural but certain. Calvin explains why the conviction of safety is now more widely extended, even to lower things: he who is persuaded of God’s kindness towards him is able to stand firm in the heaviest afflictions, which usually harass men in no small degree and for various reasons, because they interpret them as tokens of God’s wrath, or think themselves to be forsaken by him. On the quotation he says the testimony adds no small weight to the subject, for it intimates that the dread of death is so far from being a reason for our falling away that it has been almost ever the lot of God’s servants to have death as it were present before their eyes; and he thinks it probable that in that psalm the miserable oppression of the people under a former tyranny is described. On the victory he says he has retained the apostle’s own compound word, and reports the renderings of others, that we are more than victors, that we do more than overcome, and that we most fully overcome, noting that the apostle commonly uses the preposition in an intensive sense, so that the meaning is that we always struggle and always emerge.

Clarke says he thinks this question has been generally misunderstood, and refers it to the persecutions and tribulations to which genuine Christians were exposed through their attachment to Christ, and to the gracious provision God had made for their support and final salvation. On the quotation he says these things are no more than we may naturally expect from the present constitution of the world and from the positive predictions of the prophet, who foresaw that a wicked world would always persecute and oppress the true followers of God. On the victory he draws the answer out of the psalm itself: as the prophet adds in the same place that all this is come upon us, yet have we not forgotten thee nor dealt falsely in thy covenant, so all these things may happen to us, but in all these things we are more than conquerors, abiding faithful in the new covenant of our God, who is faithful that has promised. On the persuasion he sets it after experience rather than before it: after the blessed experience we have had of support by the grace and Spirit of him that loved us, he is persuaded that neither fear of death, nor hope of life, nor evil angels, nor principalities, nor powers persecuting us for Christ’s sake, nor the things we endure at present, nor the things to come, whatever tribulation we may be called to suffer, shall be able to separate us. Wesley observes that the list proceeds in order from lesser troubles to greater, and asks whether any of these can separate us from his protection in the trouble and, if he sees good, from deliverance out of it. On the quotation he glosses all the day as meaning every day, continually, and notes that we are so accounted both by our enemies and by ourselves. On the victory he says we more than conquer, being not only no losers but abundant gainers by all these trials, and thinks this period seems to describe the full assurance of hope.

Barnes takes the question as asking who shall finally or entirely separate us, and calls it a new argument showing the apostle’s strong confidence in the safety of the Christian. On the disputed phrase he is candid: the expression is ambiguous and may mean either our love to Christ or his love to us, and he understands it in the former sense, supposing it to mean our love toward him. On the quotation he says the passage is quoted not as having originally reference to Christians but as aptly descriptive of their condition, since the condition of saints in the time of the psalmist was similar to that of Christians in the time of Paul and the same language would express both. On the victory he explains that we gain the victory in the very midst of these things, while we are enduring them, since they have not power to subdue us, to alienate our love and confidence, or to produce apostasy. On the persuasion he says the expression implies unwavering certainty, the Latin version rendering it that he is certain, and expounds the first pair as neither the fear of death nor all the pains and tortures of the dying scene, nor on the other hand the hope of life. Ellicott states the disputed phrase in a line, that it is the love which Christ has for us and not that which we have for Christ, and remarks that the Apostle is speaking from his own actual experience. On the quotation he dates the psalm to some period of great national distress, at what precise period the data do not enable us to say, but probably not earlier than Josiah, and lays down the principle that the sufferings of God’s people at all times are typical of each other. On the victory he says that so far from being vanquished we are conquerors, and that when we are weak then are we strong. On the persuasion he says the enumeration which follows is intended to include, poetically rather than logically, every possible category of being, and especially those unseen powers of evil against which the warfare of the Christian was more particularly directed, comparing the wrestling against principalities described in the letter to the Ephesians. Robertson parses the future active of an old verb derived through an adverb from the word for space, and asks whether anyone can put a distance between Christ’s love and us, or lead Christ to cease loving us, noting that the apostle changes from asking who to asking what. On the quotation he notes the present passive of the verb and finds the same idea of continuous martyrdom in the first letter to the Corinthians. On the victory he calls the compound a late and rare formation occurring here alone in the New Testament, and renders it that we gain a surpassing victory through the one who loved us. On the persuasion he parses the perfect passive and renders it that he stands convinced, observing that the items mentioned are those that people dread, namely life, death, supernatural powers above and below, and any creature at all to cover any omissions.

Theodoret handles the passage briefly and turns each part into a practical conclusion. On the quotation he says the witness adduced is exactly correspondent to the subject in hand, for it was spoken in the persons of those who had the same object, since the thrice-holy Spirit wrote that psalm by the inspired David concerning men in the same case; the fitness of the citation is therefore not a matter of verbal resemblance but of a shared situation before God. On the victory he grounds the whole confidence on a comparison which he states as a matter of consistency rather than of feeling: opposing the love which God bears us to all these things, we rise superior to afflictions, for we reckon that it were most absurd for our Lord Christ to have undergone death for sinners, and yet for ourselves not most readily to embrace martyrdom for him. The argument is thus not that the sufferings are light but that the disproportion between what he bore and what we are asked to bear settles the question in advance. Cyril of Jerusalem puts the verse into the mouth of the believer facing the last adversary: the Lord, knowing the greatness of that enemy, grants indulgence to the godly by telling those in Judaea to flee to the mountains, but if any man is conscious that he is stout-hearted enough to encounter Satan, let him stand, for Cyril does not despair of the Church’s nerves, and let him say, Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?

debates: Whether the love of Christ means his love to us or ours to him: Gill denies outright that the saints’ love is meant, since though their love can never be destroyed it may be abated and cannot be the ground of the security, and Ellicott states the same in a line; Barnes, however, calls the expression ambiguous and understands it in the other sense, of our love toward Christ, while Clarke thinks the question has been generally misunderstood and refers it to the persecutions endured for Christ’s sake
